item.title: Republicans Recoil as Duffy Outlines $50 Billion Request for Air Traffic Improvements
item.description:
The Trump administration on Tuesday laid out its rationale for requesting an additional $50.1 billion to fully modernize the air traffic control system, which Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, demanded in the aftermath of Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

It didn’t seem to go over well.

“I’m not going to vote for that,” said Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, emerging from a Senate G.O.P. lunch with Mr. Duffy.

Too many parts of Mr. Duffy’s funding request had nothing to do with air traffic control, Mr. Kennedy said, while calling the secretary’s decision to use Friday’s debacle as a reason to increase his funding demands “a huge mistake.”

When Mr. Duffy unveiled plans to overhaul the Federal Aviation Administration’s air traffic control system in the spring of 2025, he estimated that the project would cost about $30 billion. Last summer, Congress approved $12.5 billion as an initial investment in the effort; Mr. Duffy has been urging lawmakers to commit additional funds to see it through.

This fall, the secretary backed a new plan to combine air traffic control upgrades with airport improvements, asking Congress for a $30 billion investment to cover the expanded project.

But minutes after Friday’s ground stop ended, he raised that request to $50 billion while discussing the halt in air traffic on camera.

“I’ve asked, the president’s asked for $30 billion; I want $50 billion,” he told reporters from a podium at the White House. The new request surprised lawmakers.

The F.A.A. had halted thousands of flights for hours Friday after noticing that parts of the air traffic control telecommunications network were becoming overloaded. Over the weekend, the F.A.A. determined that the problems began after a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark., began blasting the system with connection requests, and similar issues emerged with another router in Texas.

It was the third ground stop in the F.A.A.’s history, and the longest to have resulted from a technical issue.

Mr. Duffy faced pressure to justify why he suddenly wanted $50 billion to address the air traffic control system’s woes, especially after Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, said on Saturday that the agency needed only another $10.1 billion to complete its air traffic modernization venture.

The details that Mr. Duffy, Mr. Bedford, and Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, provided to lawmakers on Tuesday were thin.

In the request, $10.1 billion would go toward air traffic equipment modernization. But only up to $2 billion of that would be dedicated to fixing the telecommunications system whose failures prompted officials to declare a ground stop.

Another $20 billion of the request would go to renovating air traffic control towers and centers. The remaining $20 billion in the proposal is dedicated to airport improvements, which several senators argued shouldn’t be the federal government’s concern.

Those funds, the letter’s authors wrote, would help the administration “to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network.”

Mr. Duffy has challenged Congress to approve funding before the end of the year, when control of Congress will shift from the Republicans to the Democrats.

Yet many Republicans senators were unconvinced that taxpayers should foot that bill.

“Let the airline industry pay for it,” Senator Rick Scott, Republican of Florida, told reporters after hearing Mr. Duffy’s pitch. “They’re the ones going to use this.”

Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas and the chairman of the committee that oversees the F.A.A., told reporters outside the Capitol on Tuesday that “the odds are quite high that there will be a meaningful investment in additional air traffic control technology improvements.”

Asked what he thought about the other $40 billion in the request, Mr. Cruz responded that “we’re focused on the safety investments.”

Mr. Duffy appeared to acknowledge the skepticism he encountered from Republicans, telling reporters after the lunch with senators on Tuesday that he would defer to the lawmakers’ budgeting process, and that ultimately, “I’ll take what I can get.”

But his efforts to appeal his case to lawmakers didn’t appear to win him any clear support.

“I still don’t understand how $30 billion became $50 billion,” said Senator Rand Paul, Republican of Kentucky, adding: “We shouldn’t just throw money at a problem.”

item.title: I.R.S. Opens Criminal Probes as Part of Trump’s Pursuit of Left-Wing Groups
item.description:
The Internal Revenue Service has initiated at least four criminal investigations as part of the Trump administration’s crackdown on left-wing groups that began after the killing of Charlie Kirk last year, according to an internal agency memorandum viewed by The New York Times.

The pages of the memo viewed by The Times do not identify the subjects of the investigations, nor is their current status known. But even the existence of the criminal investigations is the clearest sign yet that President Trump has successfully dragged the typically technocratic I.R.S. into enforcing his political agenda.

The memo describes the work done by a group of a dozen I.R.S. officials detailed to a task force formed in response to Mr. Kirk’s death on Sept. 10, 2025. Mr. Trump ordered agencies across the government to investigate the antifascist movement, or antifa, and other groups that espouse “extremism on migration, race and gender,” among other views.

Under that order, the I.R.S. was told to investigate whether nonprofits were “directly or indirectly financing political violence or domestic terrorism.” In March, officials from the criminal investigations branch of the service began working with the task force out of the F.B.I. headquarters.

The I.R.S. work on the task force has also involved rapid response to events like protests at Delaney Hall, an immigrant detention center in Newark, N.J., the memo states. Protesters and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have repeatedly clashed at the site, and a Democratic member of Congress is among the people who have been charged with a crime after an encounter with federal agents there.

I.R.S. officials reviewed financial information, including subpoenaed Venmo records, about people arrested during those protests, as well as businesses that the officials believed could be funding them. At one point, I.R.S. officials used facial recognition and tattoo analysis databases to help identify individuals, the memo said.

Many nonprofits and their tax lawyers have feared that the I.R.S., with its vast stores of financial information and power to enforce tax law, could become a potent tool in the president’s vendetta against liberal organizations. That concern began last year, when Mr. Trump publicly called for the I.R.S. to strip elite universities and other nonprofits of their tax-exempt status, a move that would upend their finances.

But because audits and tax investigations are protected under federal taxpayer privacy law, it has been unclear to what extent the I.R.S. has heeded the Trump administration’s push to scrutinize left-leaning groups. The memo viewed by The Times is the first window into the work the I.R.S. has actually undertaken to carry out the demands from the White House.

The internal status report, circulated among leaders in I.R.S. Criminal Investigation, describes the activities of the I.R.S. team on the task force between March and July of this year. The Times viewed the first six pages of the eight-page memo and did not view its two-page appendix identifying the targets of the I.R.S. investigations. One focus for the group is investigating people who doxx or threaten government officials, the memo states.

A spokesman for the I.R.S. said the agency’s criminal branch “has collaborated with federal law enforcement agencies, including the F.B.I., to investigate individuals and entities that may be funding domestic terrorism or political violence.”

In addition to the four criminal investigations mentioned in the memo, the group of I.R.S. special agents and analysts have also referred at least four tax-exempt groups to the civil side of the agency that conducts audits, the memo said. The document said that the group of I.R.S. officials had been assigned to nine grand juries and helped the F.B.I. with financial analysis, including of whether groups had improperly filled out Form 990, the main tax form for nonprofits.

The Trump administration has cast its focus on “domestic terrorism” as a way to prevent political violence, but its enforcement campaign has only fueled fears about the federal government’s penalizing lawful political activity. In the days after Mr. Kirk’s killing, the Justice Department pushed U.S. attorneys to investigate George Soros’s Open Society foundation, a major donor to liberal causes.

And in the spring, the government charged the Southern Poverty Law Center, a nonprofit group that has long tracked hate groups, with defrauding its donors. Prosectors have charged Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man, with killing Mr. Kirk and have not accused him of working with any outside group.

Within the I.R.S., officials have discussed the creation of a new process for revoking the tax-exempt status of nonprofit groups, according to three people familiar with the change. Organizations that have been indicted or have had senior members of their leadership indicted would face an expedited audit, conducted in a matter of months, that could result in the loss of their tax-exempt status, the people said. But I.R.S. lawyers have raised concerns about the legal rigor of such a process, and the agency has so far not implemented it.

Beyond the Delaney Hall protests, the I.R.S. detail to the F.B.I. task force has also helped work on the federal law enforcement response to the shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in the spring, as well as a shooting at a mosque in San Diego in May. The I.R.S. group also assisted with the Ultimate Fighting Championship event that Mr. Trump hosted on the White House lawn in June, though its exact role is unclear.

But much of the memo viewed by The Times describes the bureaucratic challenges the I.R.S. officials have faced working with the F.B.I. The “continual turnover” of F.B.I. leadership on the task force and the bureau’s “culture of lack of information sharing” has made it difficult for the I.R.S. to establish itself in the task force, the memo stated. An F.B.I. spokesman did not respond to a request for comment.

The I.R.S. memo, which is unsigned, describes how, overall, opportunities for the group have been limited. Some potential financial crimes have been identified, the memo states, but they are not related to the task force’s work “because there was no specific threat directed at a government entity, its property or a government employee.” In some instances, other I.R.S. agents ignored emails from the task force or did not inform the group that they were already working a case, the memo said.

The I.R.S. group recommends that it be given a broader remit to focus more squarely on “investigating the misuse of 501(c)(3) organizations and/or individuals with nexus to terrorism,” referring to the tax code section that applies to many nonprofits. Under federal law, any organization that the federal government officially identifies as a terrorist group immediately loses its tax-exempt status.

With roughly 3,000 employees, the criminal investigation branch of the I.R.S. is a relatively small slice of the agency overall. But it has been frequently deployed as part of broader Trump administration initiatives. An inspector general report this year detailed the time I.R.S. criminal agents spent patrolling the streets of Washington and Memphis, Tenn., as part of the administration’s law enforcement efforts there. That came at the expense of work on criminal tax investigations, the inspector general found.

item.title: Man Indicted in Bomb Threat at Illinois Ethanol Plant
item.description:
A federal grand jury in Illinois indicted a man on Tuesday on charges of threatening to detonate an explosive device at a Peoria ethanol plant.

The man, Andrew Kozak, was charged with two felonies in connection with a bomb threat at the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant that led to a lengthy evacuation in Peoria last week.

Emergency workers found and deactivated one device at the plant on Friday, though the charges against Mr. Kozak do not specifically accuse him of placing that device. Mr. Kozak was indicted on two felony counts — threats regarding explosives and interstate communications of a threat — which could carry years in prison if he is convicted.

A LinkedIn profile for an Andrew Kozak in the Peoria area listed him as an employee of BioUrja, where it said he had worked since February. Company officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Court records did not indicate whether Mr. Kozak had hired a lawyer. Officials at the federal public defender’s office in the Central District of Illinois did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The indictment was sparse on details but said that Mr. Kozak “sent an email to BioUrja which indicated that explosive devices had been placed” at the Peoria facility. Mr. Kozak was scheduled to make an initial court appearance in U.S. District Court in Peoria on Tuesday afternoon. The indictment did not describe a motive for the threats.

While crews searched the plant for more explosives on Friday and Saturday, events were canceled, roads were blocked, and residents within a one-mile radius of the plant were told to evacuate. The search for additional explosives concluded on Saturday without any being located, and residents were allowed to return home. No injuries were reported.

Ernesto Londoño and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Hegseth Nominates His Former Aide to Lead the Army
item.description:
After more than six months of delay, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to lead the Army.

Mr. Hegseth fired the Army’s previous chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, in April without explanation. That dismissal, along with the departure of Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll in August, has left the Army essentially rudderless as it struggles to adapt to the threat posed by cheap, deadly drones and missiles that have pounded U.S. bases in the Middle East.

General LaNeve, who previously worked as Mr. Hegseth’s senior military aide, is now serving dual roles as the Army’s acting chief of staff and its vice chief. Mr. Hegseth nominated Lt. Gen. Marcus S. Evans to serve as the vice chief of staff.

Their nominations were sent initially to the White House for President Trump’s approval. Earlier this week the White House forwarded the nominations to the Senate Armed Services Committee, congressional officials said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel moves.

“For 36 years, I’ve served in the U.S. Army, currently as the vice chief of staff,” General LaNeve said in a statement. “I’m deeply honored by the president’s trust and confidence for the nomination to serve as the chief of staff of the U.S. Army, and, if confirmed, I look forward to continuing to serve our soldiers, their families and our nation.”

In most cases, senior military leaders who are nominated to lead their services are easily confirmed by the Senate. But it is not clear that General LaNeve’s nomination can muster the necessary votes to advance, officials said.

General LaNeve was widely thought to be Mr. Hegseth’s top choice for the job, but the uncertainty surrounding support for his nomination has delayed the Pentagon from sending it forward. The Republican rout in the midterm elections could make General LaNeve’s confirmation even less likely next year.

Still, he must overcome serious doubts from G.O.P. lawmakers who are frustrated with the way Mr. Hegseth has led the Pentagon and who are reluctant to vote for senior officers with close ties to the secretary.

Senator Joni Ernst, an Iowa Republican who deployed to Iraq and served 22 years in the National Guard, has voiced repeated skepticism about General LaNeve. Earlier this year, she suggested three alternatives to the White House. Her top choice was Gen. Christopher T. Donahue, who was serving as the top Army officer in Europe before Mr. Hegseth forced him to retire, officials said.

Some lawmakers have quietly expressed hope that General Donahue could return to active duty if Mr. Hegseth were impeached or forced to resign. For now, though, Mr. Hegseth’s job seems safe.

Last week, House Republicans banded together to shelve an effort to impeach Mr. Hegseth, shielding him from a damaging rebuke and a potential ouster. Democrats have vowed to make another effort to impeach Mr. Hegseth in January when they will have a majority in Congress.

The next few weeks will be critical for Mr. Hegseth, who will be pushing lawmakers to approve as much as $350 billion in new defense spending. The Pentagon badly needs that money to continue paying for the war with Iran and Mr. Trump’s ambitious modernization program.

Mr. Hegseth’s decision to nominate General LaNeve, despite the doubts about his fitness for the Army chief job, suggests that Mr. Hegseth is not chastened by the looming threat of impeachment and plans to continue to fight for his and Mr. Trump’s priorities.

item.title: A Death Along Lake Superior Revives Memories of ‘the Gales of November’
item.description:
On the morning of Nov. 6, something was moving in the surf along the Upper Peninsula of Michigan.

A man walking his dog along the beach looked more closely: It was a body.

Lake Superior had just given up its latest casualty.

The shores of the largest of the Great Lakes are scenic. They are also blustery, and the danger they pose to human life becomes pronounced during each year’s 11th month. Lake Superior’s shoreline communities commemorate the grim toll of shipwrecks and lives claimed by its waters, which become a cauldron of wild and deadly storms during the fall season, known in folklore — and a Gordon Lightfoot song — as “the gales of November.”

Winds barrel across the surface of Lake Superior at speeds that conjure the gusts of a hurricane. Waves two dozen feet high or more roll through open water, or crash over shoreline cliffs.

The body found near the shores of Harvey, Mich., was identified by the police as a 62-year-old man from Calumet, a village about 70 miles away. The man’s survivors requested that he not be identified. The Marquette Police Department, working from witness reports, believed he had been seized by the waves a day before when Superior’s powerful currents pounded Black Rocks, an outcropping of volcanic basalt where he had gone to take photographs.

Snatched from the surface, like too many before him, on decades of windy November days.

Lake Superior is the deepest of the Great Lakes, and is typically considered the largest body of freshwater in the world, with a surface area of more than 31,000 square miles. Depending on the season, its edges lap or pummel the shores of Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Ontario.

Its cliffs, forests and rugged shores are striking, and it is a major artery for the workhorses of maritime shipping that move cargo through interlocking waterways to the ocean and ports thousands of miles away.

But the tempests of Lake Superior have overtaken hundreds of ships. Its routes and shoreline points have earned reputations as maritime graveyards.

The lake earned its most fearsome legacy on Nov. 10, 1975, when a 729-foot freighter, the Edmund Fitzgerald, sank in a calamitous storm that was enshrined in Mr. Lightfoot’s ballad “The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald.”

Twenty-nine crew members and the ship vanished beneath the waves.

The tragedy has become a touchstone for lake communities every November, when the gales descend. The recent drowning death fell days before annual commemorations for the ship’s crew.

In Paradise, Mich., the Great Lakes Shipwreck Museum livestreamed a memorial for the descendants of the Fitzgerald’s crew.

In Detroit, the Rev. Todd Meyer of the Mariners’ Church pulled the rope on the church bell 29 times, once for each crew member.

“We have been doing this for 51 years,” he said.

In Minnesota, the fate of the 62-year-old man was incorporated into the ceremony for the ship’s crew at the Split Rock Lighthouse, where the names of the crew members were read aloud.

Hayes Scriven, the site manager of the lighthouse, said in a speech that the death, along with those from other shipwrecks and rescues, was “a sobering reminder of the power of the lake.”

“A lot of us around the lake, involved in the Fitz memorials, talk about how the Fitz crew itself can stand as a memorial for all of the people that are lost on Lake Superior and the Great Lakes,” he said in an interview.

The Marquette Fire Department called the latest drowning “a sad, harsh reminder of Lake Superior’s power.”

Its crosscurrents, massive waves and turbulent waters can render its name misleading, said the fire chief, Ian Davis.

“It is really not a lake,” Chief Davis said in an interview. “It is an inland sea.”

Lake Superior becomes “more of a tempest” when large, low-pressure systems form in October and November, said Ketzel Levens, a forecaster with the National Weather Service in Duluth, Minn.

The season is often described by meteorologists as unstable when the summer water temperature is warmer on average compared with the arrival of the cold air, she said.

Those factors “create these really, really strong winds,” Ms. Levens said. “And depending on what direction they are coming, they might run across Lake Superior for potentially hundreds of miles.”

Waves propelled to shallower depths rear up to break along the shore, sometimes swamping high cliffs.

“As tall as the wave is, it is about as deep,” she said.

On the day the Calumet man went missing, the lake had been living up to its seasonal reputation of battering winds and bullying waves.

The National Weather Service in Marquette had issued a gale warning. Winds picked up by 1 p.m., with a buoy registering waves of 15.5 feet, Ben Warren, a Weather Service meteorologist in Marquette, said.

Those waves were some of the highest recorded since Oct. 24, 2017, when they measured almost 30 feet, he said.

On that day, two friends, Robert Anderson, 53, and Sarah Hall, 37, went to Black Rocks to take photographs.

Like others before them and since, they were swept away.

Mr. Anderson’s body washed up about a month later in a nearby harbor.

Ms. Hall’s body has never been found.

Unruly conditions, including on the day of the latest death, can keep divers, helicopters and boats grounded.

Still, Capt. Ryan Grim, the police chief in Marquette, said witnesses told rescuers that some people tried to help the man who was claimed by the lake.

“They actually tried to throw a jacket out to him,” he said.

item.title: Ukraine Talks Run Up Against Deep Enmity Between Russia and Europe
item.description:
When President Trump’s envoys met with President Vladimir V. Putin at the Kremlin last week, the Russian leader questioned whether Europe actually wanted to end the war in Ukraine, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting.

As evidence, Mr. Putin referred to a frequent Russian talking point about a moment early in the conflict, according to one of the people: the claim, denied by Ukraine’s leader, that European countries blocked a peace deal negotiated in Istanbul in March 2022. The Americans — Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, and Steve Witkoff, the president’s special envoy — pushed back, describing the Europeans as constructive in seeking peace, the person said.

As Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner push on in their marathon diplomacy to resolve the nearly five-year-old war, their task has been complicated by Mr. Putin’s deep hostility toward Europe, and Europe’s intense suspicion of Russia.

Having Russia and Europe agree on a postwar security arrangement on the continent, the Americans have argued, could lay the groundwork for Mr. Putin to end his war. But the prospect of achieving such an agreement appears tenuous, at best — particularly after Russia opened the current talks with an aggressive demand that NATO pull back forces from its eastern flank.

Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are not expected to participate in Mr. Trump’s scheduled meeting on Thursday with Mr. Putin and Xi Jinping, China’s leader, in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, even though the two envoys have spearheaded U.S. diplomacy with the Russian leader.

Instead, according to a U.S. official familiar with the plans, Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner will travel to Berlin to meet with an eight-member negotiating team on Thursday that European countries recently designated to represent them in talks with Russia and Ukraine. The official, like others with knowledge of the negotiations, spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.

The Trump administration has been heavily criticized for its diplomacy, even by the president’s own party. Senator Tom Cotton, Republican of Arkansas, said that Moscow’s demands showed again that Mr. Putin was “not serious about a negotiated peace.”

“Further talks are a farce at this point,” Mr. Cotton said on social media. “Putin will only agree to stop the war when he knows he can’t win. We need to help Ukraine prove that point.”

Administration officials say they are making progress, coordinating closely with Ukraine and Europe, and need to engage Russia to eventually end the war.

“The press has reported some of the maximalist positions proposed by both sides,” Mr. Kushner said on social media over the weekend. “In our private discussions, both sides understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war.”

Mr. Putin’s enmity toward Ukraine’s allies in Europe — governments that have become that country’s primary financial and political backers after Mr. Trump dialed back U.S. support — runs so deep that it is not clear whether he is even prepared to allow his negotiators to sit down with the European team. Mr. Putin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, said Monday that “a great deal would have to be done” before Europe could join the talks among Russia, Ukraine and the United States.

Officials from the three countries met face-to-face last week for the first time since February in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates. In those negotiations, Russian officials made clear that they sought a fundamental revision of what they called Europe’s “security architecture,” or reducing NATO’s presence on the continent and granting Moscow a region of influence akin to the Cold War era.

In addition to demanding a Western military rollback, Russia said the European Union and NATO needed to cease classifying Russia “as an adversary or threat,” according to a copy of a paper outlining Russia’s position that was obtained by The New York Times. It also called on NATO and European Union countries to officially renounce “their course towards inflicting a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia,” language that echoed Mr. Putin’s frequent rhetoric depicting support of Ukraine as part of a Western plan to destroy his country.

People involved in the talks said it summarized Russia’s hard-line, opening position, which could still be softened as the negotiations continue. The one-page document also called for the improvement of “incident-prevention mechanisms,” especially in the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea, to reduce the risk of unintended conflict.

As a Russian official, Vladimir Medinsky, read out some of the country’s demands in the Abu Dhabi meeting, Mr. Kushner cut in to ask what reciprocal steps Russia would take to reduce tensions, according to two people familiar with the talks. The Russians said they would work on that, the people said.

European leaders, especially from countries like Poland on NATO’s eastern flank, have described Russia’s demands as an unacceptable threat to their security. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said they were delusional for a country bogged down on the battlefield. “To propose ideas on that scale,” he wrote in a social media post, “you first need to win a world war.”

Still, European governments have responded to the Trump administration’s efforts to engage with Mr. Putin on broader issues of European security, despite deep doubts that they will work. Kaja Kallas, the bloc’s top diplomat, said at a news conference on Monday that “there are still no signs of Moscow preparing for peace.”

Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff spoke Monday to Mr. Ushakov, the Putin aide, and separately to Ukrainian officials and the new European negotiating team, which involves senior officials from the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Poland; two European Union bodies; and NATO. Mr. Kushner said in his social media post that “we are making progress” toward a “lasting peace.”

Ukrainian officials will join the Europeans and Americans for Thursday’s meeting in Berlin, which will cover postwar economic and security support for Ukraine, as well as preparation for negotiations with Russia, the U.S. official familiar with the envoys’ plans said. Senior officials traveling with Mr. Trump in China this week — Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Stephen Miller, the White House chief of staff — have been briefed on the Kushner-Witkoff talks, the U.S. official said.

The administration’s diplomatic push reflects the Trump administration’s new attempt to address Russia’s broader European security demands as part of the peace negotiations, rather than focusing only on Ukraine. For Russia, analysts say, the goal will be to use those negotiations to weaken Ukraine’s ties with Europe as much as possible — ties that Russia’s invasion has only ended up strengthening.

The Russians “were never going to end the war without a European security discussion,” said Jeremy Shapiro, a former State Department official who is now a research director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Washington. “The fact that they failed to conquer Ukraine means that the key thing they have to do is regulate the Ukrainian-Western relationship.”

Andrew E. Kramer contributed reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine, and Jeanna Smialek from Brussels.

item.title: A.I. Helps Find Major Security Bug in Java, a Software Platform Vital to the Internet
item.description:
A cybersecurity start-up revealed on Tuesday it had used a new A.I. model to uncover a critical software bug in Java, a popular programming language that is used by government agencies and about 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies.

It was the latest evidence of a reality facing companies and the government, as A.I. is revolutionizing the field of discovery in computer vulnerabilities, identifying flaws in code so rapidly that cybersecurity professionals are struggling to keep up.

Using leading A.I. models, the start-up Calif has now unearthed a string of serious vulnerabilities in recent months. The start-up’s latest effort exposed a flaw, using OpenAI’s recently released GPT-6 Cyber model, in Java, which is widely used by banks, hospitals, the aviation industry and technology giants, as well as government agencies, including those with national security missions.

“Java is the beating heart of the modern economy,” said Bruce Dang, a senior researcher at Calif. “Practically speaking, all major companies” will be affected by the bug, he added.

Mr. Dang and his colleagues have worked in recent days to coordinate with all government agencies in the intelligence-sharing alliance known as Five Eyes — which consists of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain — and major vendors in the private sector, including Google and Microsoft.

The National Security Agency, whose classified network went down on Tuesday for what it described as “routine software maintenance,” did not respond to a request for comment. It was not clear whether that disruption was related to addressing the Java bug.

Oracle, the owner of the Java trademark and provider of commercial Java licenses, did not respond to a request for comment. The company released a software patch Tuesday.

Announcements about exploits from Calif and other groups using A.I. tools have startled the cybersecurity world and upended what was considered achievable by a small band of coders just a few months ago. Those efforts, which involve working with A.I. models before they are publicly released, help alert network defenders to undetected problems in order to fix them before malicious hackers find them and wreak havoc.

But the Java discovery may be Calif’s most serious yet, one that could enable a hacker to gain remote access to sensitive internal systems. It comes on the heels of a cascade of seemingly independent disruptions in recent days — outages of Microsoft products, a nationwide grounding of flights and banking interruptions — that have shaken public confidence in the reliability of everyday technology and fanned fears that A.I. may be to blame. (So far, the explanations for each appear to be relatively benign.)

A.I.-assisted bug hunting and cyberattack building has made it much easier to identify weaknesses in systems, Mr. Whitehouse said. “We have seen this taking shape for some time, with A.I. being used to discover a growing number of latent vulnerabilities across software and the digital services we all rely on.”

The Java vulnerability is the second major bug Calif has unearthed with the aid of OpenAI models in the past few weeks after its discovery last month of a security flaws in PHP, a programming language estimated to be used by 70 percent of websites and apps on the internet.

The PHP disclosure set off fears around the world about significant disruptions for consumers and businesses and a mad scramble by companies to patch PHP before hackers could pounce. Government agencies, including the N.S.A., warned businesses to take websites offline if they could not immediately deploy a patch. Disruptions ultimately proved less serious than some predicted, however, as it became clear hackers could not easily reverse-engineer the attack method.

But PHP chiefly concerned software that helps websites function. In contrast, Java helps power the nuts and bolts of the modern digital world, including cloud computing architecture, identity management tools, email services and more.

“Java is everywhere,” said Thai Duong, the chief executive of Calif. He noted that the Java bug was not easy to weaponize into an attack, giving defenders more time to patch the issues.

“But vulnerabilities have a very long tail,” he added, predicting the bug could be a threat to systems that do not update in the next five to 10 years.

Among the most significant findings, Calif demonstrated that it could use this bug to break into Keycloak, a widely used authentication and log in system. Keycloak protects thousands of organizations, including CERN, Hewlett Packard, UnitedHealthcare and NASA.

Quang Luong, a security researcher from Calif, discovered the bug in Java’s base64 decoder, a common algorithm that is used to translate binary computer data into a legible palette of text that includes lowercase and uppercase letters, numbers and punctuation. On certain computers, researchers found that Java encounters a bug when it tries to decode 64 “A” characters followed by one equal sign:

AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=

This bug, called Java4Shell, causes Java to erroneously execute code by tampering with a section of computer memory, which typically causes the program to immediately crash. With the help of A.I., Calif researchers demonstrated that they could corrupt data by carefully arranging the memory — a technique called “heap grooming” — granting them full unauthorized access to the underlying system.

The New York Times independently verified Calif’s discovery after the start-up shared proof-of-concept details about the attack. The successful test took less than an hour.

The rapid advances with artificial intelligence in cybersecurity efforts mirror what the chess world champion Garry Kasparov observed after he lost a match to IBM’s Deep Blue computer nearly 30 years ago.

The best games of chess would not be played by humans or computers, he predicted, but by a hybrid of the two. The concept, which he called a “centaur” in a nod to the mythological half-human, half-horse creature, took off. For years, centaurs were seen as the best chess players, reaching new heights in the game.

Now companies and the government are contending with the threat of the “centaur hacker” — half A.I., half human, and fully capable of creating chaos on the internet.

The most alarming discoveries — for now, at least — still require human expertise. In recent months, small teams of veteran security researchers have used top-shelf A.I. models to build in days or hours the kinds of advanced cyberattacks that once took platoons of elite hackers at spy agencies like the National Security Agency months to construct.

Fouad Matin, who leads cyber preparedness and safety at OpenAI, said Calif’s Java research “shows how A.I. can assist expert security researchers with finding serious flaws in software we all depend on” and helps lead to collaborative fixes. “We want more security teams to have these capabilities and tools to help make critical software more secure for everyone,” Mr. Matin said.

Eduardo Vela Nava, an information security engineer at Google, said that “once notified, we swiftly rolled out mitigations and patches across Google services, developed detection to ensure there was no exploitation of the vulnerability, and provided guidance to our customers.”

Security experts expect those risks are likely to grow, at least in the short term. For about 20 years, centaur chess players were widely seen as capable of playing the best game of chess. But eventually, the centaurs were eclipsed by more advanced supercomputers.

Mr. Duong believes it may be only a matter of time until A.I. can independently build the most advanced cyberattacks, which could usher in a new age of unpredictable problems. The F.B.I. this week issued an alert warning that hackers were using new autonomous A.I. hacking tools to target government agencies and businesses around the world.

“I don’t know how much time we have — maybe three months, maybe three years,” Mr. Duong said. “But right now, the best hacker is the centaur hacker.”

item.title: With House Democratic Majority Still Growing, Recounts Are Starting in Closest Races
item.description:
House candidates in North Carolina and Minnesota are seeking recounts in some of the last uncalled races in the nation, as the exact size of Democrats’ new majority in Congress remained undetermined two weeks after the election.

Representative Virginia Foxx, a Republican who has served in North Carolina’s Fifth District since 2005 and leads the powerful Rules Committee, filed her request on Tuesday, the deadline for such a move in her state. Her Democratic opponent, Chuck Hubbard, was leading by just over 300 votes.

Ashley Bell, a Democrat who ran in North Carolina’s 10th District, submitted her recount request on Friday. She was trailing Representative Pat Harrigan, a Republican who has served the district since last year, by more than 2,500 votes on Tuesday — a margin not typically reversed by recount. Mr. Harrigan said in a statement that he respected her right to request a recount.

The two North Carolina candidates join Representative Brad Finstad, a Republican in Minnesota’s First District, who said last week that he would seek a recount after the Democrat leading by about 300 votes, Jake Johnson, declared victory. Mr. Johnson later said in a statement that recounts rarely change election outcomes and that he had begun his transition to Congress.

These recounts, all in Republican-leaning districts, will add another step in the process of determining the makeup of the new Congress. Among the House races called by Tuesday afternoon, Democrats had 257 seats, one short of surpassing the majority the party secured in 2008.

Seven House races have not yet been called by The Associated Press, two of which are in North Carolina. Democrats tied their 2008 total on Tuesday when The Associated Press called a third North Carolina race, in the state’s Third District, where Raymond Smith, a former state lawmaker, defeated Representative Greg Murphy, a Republican who took office in 2019 and conceded last Wednesday.

A candidate in a non-statewide election in North Carolina, such as a House race, can demand a recount after the county canvass, which was Friday, if the margin is no greater than 1 percent of the total votes cast, according to the state’s election rules.

The process in North Carolina, paid for by the county boards, will begin with a full machine recount. The candidate who trails after that will then have 24 hours to request a hand recount of a random sample of the votes, to rule out discrepancies between the machine recount and hand count.

If the results of the sample recount differed enough from the machine recount to affect the outcome, the State Board of Elections would order a full hand recount of the ballots, according to the board.

“In a race where no candidate received a majority of the votes, it is necessary that we take every measure to ensure the ballot count is accurate,” Ms. Foxx said in an emailed statement on Monday, ahead of her official recount request, calling the margin between her and Mr. Hubbard, a former journalist, “razor thin.”

Minnesota allows for publicly funded recounts in federal races if the difference in the number of votes cast for the leader and another candidate is less than 0.25 percent of the total vote. A recount request can be submitted between Thursday and next Monday, according to the Minnesota secretary of state. The recount would take place from Nov. 30 to Dec. 4.

Mr. Finstad’s lawyers have spoken to the secretary of state’s office about his intention to request a recount, said Cassondra Knudson, a spokeswoman for the office. Mr. Finstad’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Johnson, a former high school math teacher, appeared confident that his lead over Mr. Finstad would hold, traveling to Washington last week to attend orientation meetings for new members of Congress.

“Really looking forward to hitting the ground running starting Jan. 3,” he said in a video from the Capitol posted on Friday.

Elsewhere, at least two House races were called last week after recounts.

Representative María Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican of Florida’s 27th District, won re-election after a recount confirmed initial results. So did Representative Joe Wilson, a Republican who has served South Carolina’s Second District since 2001. Both states have automatic recount provisions that mandate recounts if the margin of victory falls short of certain thresholds.

item.title: Waymo Pulls Its Driverless Taxis From All U.S. Highways Temporarily
item.description:
Waymo has temporarily pulled its driverless vehicles from freeways in the United States after California barred the cars from the state’s highways, the company said.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered Waymo’s driverless vehicles to stop operating and testing on all of the state’s freeways on Nov. 11, citing an “an imminent hazard to public safety.”

In a statement, the department cited an incident in which three Waymo vehicles entered a construction closure on Highway 101 and a separate episode involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Interstate 280 in San Francisco.

Waymo said it withdrew its vehicles from highways across the country the same day.

“Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state,” Chris Pappas, a Waymo spokesman, said in a statement on Tuesday. “In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance.”

The restrictions came after a video was posted on social media on Nov. 6 showing a Waymo car attempting to pass two California Highway Patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the flow of traffic on Interstate 280 in San Francisco.

The restrictions in California will remain active until the autonomous vehicle company makes “effective corrective actions,” according to the D.M.V.’s statement.

Earlier this year, Waymo had to update software in thousands of its taxis after some of them had driven into flooded roadways.

item.title: Emboldened by G.O.P. Election Losses, Iran Digs In, Officials Say
item.description:
Iran’s leaders have hardened their negotiating position with the United States since the midterm elections, seeing the sweeping Republican losses as a rebuke of President Trump’s handling of the war, according to U.S., European and Iranian officials.

The resolve in Tehran stands in contrast to the mood in Washington, where the election results have generated fresh concerns about Mr. Trump’s next moves.

Vice President JD Vance and other prominent Republicans say the war contributed to their party’s wipeout. After that comment, Mr. Trump removed Mr. Vance from the negotiating team, asking him to focus on domestic issues.

One question now is whether Mr. Trump will make another push for a diplomatic deal, renew attacks or simply walk away, pulling back the massive U.S. military force built up in the region. But it is also possible Mr. Trump’s hand could be forced, either by unilateral Israeli action or if Iran strikes U.S. interests or a partner nation first.

U.S. and European officials are divided over how seriously Iran wants to negotiate an end to the war, which the United States and Israel launched more than eight months ago. U.S. and European intelligence agencies have said the Iranian government, while emboldened, remains open to a deal if the United States allows Tehran to have access to billions of dollars of frozen assets.

Other officials note that Iran has developed plans to intensify the war to push America back to the negotiating table. That could include more attacks or stepping up strikes on tankers that do not pay the Iranian government a fee to cross through the Strait of Hormuz, which could drive fuel and other prices higher.

In an interview last week, Representative Jim Himes, the Connecticut Democrat who will become the chairman of the House Intelligence Committee next year, said Iranian officials had a sophisticated read on U.S. politics.

“The message of the election will not be lost on the regime,” Mr. Himes said. “They feel more strategically empowered against the Trump administration than they have in a long time.”

Iranian officials said Iran’s strategy to bring economic pain to American voters by closing the Strait of Hormuz had paid off.

The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, said they viewed the elections as an Iranian victory over Washington. The officials said Iran was inclined to be more defiant and offer fewer concessions in negotiations.

Indirect negotiations are still underway as governments in the region try to prevent a return to all-out war. Abbas Araghchi, the lead Iranian negotiator, was in Pakistan on Sunday and visited Oman on Monday, two countries that have served as mediators.

Mr. Himes noted that U.S. military pressure and financial sanctions had sharply reduced the number of imported goods entering Iran and had created “really severe economic pain.”

Iran’s regime was akin to a cornered animal, Mr. Himes said. “That cornered animal might seek to negotiate, but I also think it’s likely that cornered animal is going to lash out in some pretty wild ways, maybe in the service of negotiation.”

Some U.S. officials believe that another round of military strikes could push Iran’s economy closer to collapse, especially if they target energy infrastructure. Other officials said that earlier predictions about Iran’s economic collapse proved wrong.

Throughout the war, Mr. Trump has said that his primary motivation for starting it was to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb.

In July, The New York Times reported that American intelligence agencies believed that Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, was far more interested than his father and predecessor in pursuing a nuclear weapon. The new leader’s father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war in an Israeli attack aided by U.S. intelligence.

While Iran has enormous leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, with attacks on shipping that slow the flow of oil, Mr. Himes said that influence would fade. As Saudi Arabia builds more pipelines to bypass the strait, Iran’s ability to influence international oil markets will decrease, he said, one reason Iran might turn to a nuclear weapon.

Inside Iran, there are growing calls from clerics and members of Parliament for Tehran to build a nuclear weapon to prevent future attacks. The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, said this month in an address on state television that Iran had no plans to change its nuclear doctrine and weaponize its program, which it says is for civilian purposes.

Since the opening weeks of the war, Western officials have said that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps has emerged more firmly in control. There has been some speculation about how firmly the new supreme leader is in control — or even if he had been seriously injured or killed.

Western intelligence officials said they believe Mr. Khamenei’s views are closely aligned with the hard-line elements, but they now assess he is not just a figurehead.

Mr. Himes said he did not know how Mr. Khamenei conveyed his orders but was certain he had not been killed.

“The supreme leader is alive, and he is functional and operational,” he said.

If Iran restarts its attacks, it could force Mr. Trump’s hand. The United States and Israel have developed intelligence showing that Iranian officials have discussed a willingness to potentially use chemical weapons or conduct other unconventional attacks. But some U.S. officials expressed skepticism about the information.

A primary sticking point in negotiations is reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Current and former U.S. officials said that Iran wanted relief from sanctions and payments from Arab countries before it allowed ships through. The United States has insisted that Iran stop its attacks on ships before any money is unfrozen or sanctions lifted.

The sequencing of any diplomatic deal has scuttled previous rounds of talks, and officials said it could very well do so again — as Iranian negotiators dig in, believing they are facing a weakened Mr. Trump.

The midterm election results have been a hot topic on political talks shows on Iranian state television and in Iranian newspapers. “The beginning of the fall,” read one headline. “A historic warning,” said another.

Iranian officials said Mr. Vance’s comments after the vote, in which he blamed the war for his party’s losses at the polls, signaled deep divisions at the White House.

“Iran thinks Trump is under pressure from his constituents and his party to end the war with Iran,” Peiman Salehi, an analyst in Tehran who is close to the government, said in a phone interview. “So, they are not going to stand down. They have been emboldened and feeling very confident right now.”

item.title: Trump Administration Says It Will Not Use Ships to Deport Migrants
item.description:
The Trump administration has decided not to use ships to deport migrants, after the Department of Homeland Security studied using ferries and a maritime training ship called Golden Bear to transport them to Central and South America.

The acting director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement asserted in a letter on Monday to two senior Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee that ships would not be used to deport migrants from the country.

“While the agency is continually evaluating options for effective and efficient ways to carry out its mission, D.H.S. has determined it will not use ships, including training vessels or private foreign ships, for removals,” wrote the acting director, David J. Venturella. “Removal efforts will continue using air and ground transportation.”

He added that the agency was “committed to enforcing federal immigration laws in a humane, efficient manner and in compliance with federal law.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions about the decision.

Representative John Garamendi, a California Democrat whose district includes Cal Poly Maritime Academy, where Training Ship Golden Bear was docked for decades, said in a statement that the administration’s commitment was a “major win for accountability.”

The New York Times reported last month that homeland security officials had held preliminary discussions about deportations by sea and identified possible ships for the task. Mr. Garamendi and Representative Salud Carbajal, also a California Democrat, later wrote to Markwayne Mullin, the department’s secretary, demanding that the idea be “immediately discarded.” They added that the use of the Golden Bear “would be a dangerous misuse of government and taxpayer property.”

From the beginning of President Trump’s second term, the administration has sought varied and unusual paths to carry out his mass deportation agenda. That has included removing migrants from the country aboard military planes and private charter jets, sending them to unfamiliar and often dangerous third countries and housing people at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba.

The use of ships to carry out deportations to countries including El Salvador, Honduras and Venezuela would have cost millions of dollars and amounted to an escalation in the administration’s strategy. Transporting a large number of migrants aboard a ship would have presented unique logistic and security challenges.

Moving the ships through international waters and past the territory of nations where American laws do not apply could also have opened the door to legal issues. Human rights groups have said that many of the deportations carried out by the administration violated international law.

While still costing millions, the use of ships could have helped defray the expense from the Department of Homeland Security to other departments of the federal government. The Golden Bear was used for more than three decades as a classroom at sea, carrying cadets studying at the maritime academy across the Pacific Ocean. The academy said in October that the 500-foot ship was set to be transferred back to the U.S. Maritime Administration, a Transportation Department agency, to be officially decommissioned.

The Trump administration’s proposal to deport migrants by sea had conjured memories of a controversial 1950s campaign that expelled hundreds of thousands of Mexicans and included deporting people by sea. In August 1956, The Times reported that 40 passengers jumped from a ship near the Mexican city of Tampico, and five people drowned.

Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting.

item.title: Democrats Assail Kennedy After U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status
item.description:
Several prominent Democrats on Tuesday blamed the health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., for the resurgence of the measles virus in the country more than a quarter-century after its elimination, describing it as a preventable public health setback.

The criticism of Mr. Kennedy, which came from Democrats considering presidential runs as well as senators-elect, arrived soon after the Pan American Health Organization said it was revoking the country’s measles elimination status.

The organization also said on Tuesday that Bolivia and Mexico had lost their measles elimination statuses. Canada lost its status last year.

Vaccination rates started to drop during the Covid-19 pandemic and have continued to fall under the second Trump administration. Public health experts have said the Health and Human Services Department has moved slowly under President Trump to control measles outbreaks. They have criticized Mr. Kennedy for questioning childhood vaccines and promoting unproven treatments.

Democrats on Tuesday pointed at the secretary’s views on vaccines; he long criticized the measles vaccine but more recently said that all American children should receive it.

“This dangerous setback was 100% avoidable and is the result of one person: RFK Jr.” Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said in a statement. “Remove him now.”

Another potential presidential candidate, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, a state experiencing one of the country’s largest measles outbreaks, said in a statement that there was “a clear line from the misinformation, vaccine skepticism, and incompetence of RFK Jr. to this devastating news.”

And Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, a former director of the Detroit Health Department, accused Mr. Trump of “putting an anti-science grifter in charge of public health.”

In a statement on Tuesday, Mr. Kennedy reiterated his recent support for the measles vaccine and vowed to “stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status.”

“Worldwide Covid-era disruptions interrupted routine childhood vaccination, leaving gaps in protection here and abroad,” Mr. Kennedy said in the statement, noting that other countries, including Spain and Britain, had also recently lost elimination status.

“We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust,” Mr. Kennedy added. “We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.”

Mr. Kennedy was also facing criticism from at least one prominent Republican, Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a doctor and the chair of the chamber’s Health Committee. Mr. Cassidy cast a crucial vote last year to confirm Mr. Kennedy after saying that he had secured concessions from him.

“The secretary has made it part of his life’s work to undermine faith in immunizations,” Mr. Cassidy told reporters on Tuesday, adding that Mr. Kennedy had broken a promise in his confirmation hearings to not continue to erode confidence in vaccines. “Since then he’s done everything he could to undermine immunizations.”

Asked whether lawmakers should remove Mr. Kennedy, Mr. Cassidy, who is departing the Senate after being defeated by a Trump-backed primary challenger, said, “We don’t have time in this Congress.”

Mr. Kennedy ran for president in the 2024 cycle, initially as a Democrat and then as an independent. He dropped out of the race about two months before Election Day and endorsed Mr. Trump, saying that he had secured assurances that Mr. Trump would “enlist” him in his second administration. Now Mr. Kennedy is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.

Last week, Governor Beshear said he had sent a letter to Mr. Trump demanding that he fire Mr. Kennedy, citing “totally preventable” cases of measles in Kentucky. The Kentucky Department for Public Health has reported more than 200 cases of measles this year, a jump from zero in 2024.

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat who is considering a presidential run, has also called for Mr. Kennedy’s removal. Mr. Newsom said on Tuesday on social media that the United States was “losing ground against a disease we eliminated decades ago.”

The White House deferred comment to the health department, which pointed to Mr. Kennedy’s statement.

Democrats, who won majorities in the House and Senate in their best midterm performance in decades, have been considering whether to try to impeach Mr. Kennedy next year.

Representative Haley Stevens, a Michigan Democrat, brought articles of impeachment against Mr. Kennedy last year, though the push did not gain momentum. Democrats said the discussions were gaining urgency after the revocation of the measles designation on Tuesday.

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton, a centrist Democrat of Kansas, said in an interview on Tuesday that he was unsure whether he would support removing Mr. Kennedy. But he said it was “something I will be thinking about,” describing the loss of the measles elimination status as the product of Mr. Kennedy’s “waffling on vaccinations.”

Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, a Democrat and doctor, was also considering whether she’d support a move in Congress to remove Mr. Kennedy, a spokeswoman said.

“Even if leadership at HHS changed tomorrow,” Ms. Andrews said in a statement, “rebuilding that trust would take years.”

item.title: For Democrats, a Leadership Fight Is Marring an Electoral Triumph
item.description:
When Democratic senators gathered for a weekend conference call not even two weeks after winning a decisive new majority, the messy leadership fight that was dividing their ranks was not supposed to be on the agenda.

But when it was her turn to speak, Senator-elect Annie Andrews, the pediatrician who flipped a seat in South Carolina, brought up the subject that was weighing on everyone’s mind. Drawing on her medical background, she expressed dismay that a public battle over who should lead Democrats’ new majority was threatening to overshadow their enormous victory and sow discord at an inopportune time.

“It’s like, if there was a patient bleeding out in the trauma bay and the cardiothoracic surgeon and trauma surgeon were standing outside the trauma bay arguing about who was going to take the lead,” Ms. Andrews said on Tuesday, confirming remarks she made during the private call on Saturday. “When really what we need is someone just to stop the bleeding.”

The lament — coming from a Democrat who has called for generational change in leadership — underscored how the contest between Senators Chuck Schumer of New York, the party’s current leader, and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who hopes to replace him, has injected an unwelcome note of division into an otherwise triumphant moment for the party.

At a time when senators would rather focus on plans for their new majority, they are instead facing pressure from colleagues, constituents, activists and interest groups to weigh in publicly on an internal matter that is to be decided by secret ballot, and which many would prefer be waged entirely in private.

“We’re getting a lot of calls, listening to people,” Senator Tim Kaine, Democrat of Virginia, said on Tuesday. “I’m certainly talking to a lot of folks, you know, out on the road. But they’re all frustrated when I tell them I save my conversations about this with members of the caucus.”

Most Democratic senators declined to comment on the leadership fight as they left their weekly caucus luncheon meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. Mr. Kaine and several others said that the battle between Mr. Schumer and Mr. Van Hollen had not been discussed at the gathering, and that senators instead spoke about funding for the Iran war.

But senators and their aides acknowledged that their offices had been besieged by calls about the leadership election, an issue that burst into public view after Mr. Van Hollen declared in a television interview his intention to unseat Mr. Schumer.

“Leave it to the Democrats,” Senator John Hickenlooper of Colorado said on Monday. “We flip nine seats, and the person who actually helps put it all together and do all that, and all of a sudden, there’s a revolt.”

While House Democrats will choose their leaders this week, senators are not scheduled to select the next majority leader until December. The winner will need a simple majority of the caucus, or at least 28 votes out of the at least 55 the Democrats will hold in the Senate next year, including the two independents who align with them.

So far, Mr. Van Hollen has locked up the public support of at least four other senators, all of them from the party’s left flank. At least fourteen Democrats have said they will back Mr. Schumer’s continued leadership.

But with the election conducted by secret ballot, commitments can be hard to nail down, and many senators are resisting the pressure to take a public position.

A number of senators-elect have expressed skepticism of or opposition to Mr. Schumer’s leadership, but have not yet publicly committed to backing Mr. Van Hollen.

And as a number of progressive groups and Democratic activists have campaigned for Mr. Van Hollen, many senators, including Ms. Andrews and Mr. Kaine, have said they are still weighing their options.

Josh Turek, the incoming senator from Iowa, told reporters on Monday that he continued to have conversations with both candidates and would support “whoever provides those answers to me that most closely align with my common-sense, prairie-populist agenda.”

Mr. Schumer, 75, has been in charge of the caucus since 2017. Even as he helped plot Democrats’ successful effort to retake the Senate, he has been the target of many left-leaning Democrats who believe he is too moderate and of younger Democrats who say their party needs new leadership.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, a left-leaning lawmaker who has been a senator since 2017, has been conducting a strikingly public campaign for Mr. Schumer’s job. After announcing his interest in the position on MS NOW, he took part in a number of cable news interviews on Sunday. His team also created a website where they are encouraging people to sign a petition supporting him and collecting campaign donations.

So far, he has drawn backing from a handful of progressive lawmakers, some of whom have embraced his tactics. Abdul El-Sayed, the incoming senator from Michigan, said it was “healthy” for Democrats to hold their leadership discussions in public view.

“We have not seen an open Senate fight for leadership for a very long time,” Mr. El-Sayed said at an event hosted by The Atlantic. “It’s good to have these conversations as a caucus out in public.”

Still, Mr. Schumer said on Tuesday that he had already locked up the support he needed to continue in his post. “I have the votes,” he said at a news conference. “And we’re all going to roll up our sleeves and we’re going to focus on lowering costs, ending corruption.”

Some of Mr. Schumer’s backers say privately that they hope he does not “misread the message” and see their support as a signal that he can continue indefinitely. They say that Mr. Schumer could ease some internal hesitation by making it clear that these two years would be his last term as leader, even if he should decide to seek re-election in 2028.

They compare the situation to 2018, when Representative Nancy Pelosi of California quelled opposition to her continued leadership of House Democrats by announcing that she would limit herself to four more years as speaker.

But Mr. Schumer’s allies view such an announcement as a drastic move that would create a lame-duck aura around him and undermine his leadership. They also remain confident enough of their support that they do not see a need to make such a commitment at this point.

Multiple Democrats also say that Mr. Schumer needs to “step back” from being the primary spokesman for the party, allowing the newly elected freshman class to occupy the limelight as a symbol of fresh Democratic thinking and expanding the leadership team to bring in new voices. Allies of Mr. Schumer have said he seems open to all of those suggestions.

While Senate Republicans have had some recent leadership battles, Democrats have avoided them for more than three decades. The last was in 1994, when Tom Daschle of South Dakota defeated Christopher J. Dodd of Connecticut by one vote for leader.

Harry Reid, the Nevada Democrat who was Mr. Daschle’s lieutenant, quickly rounded up the votes to succeed him when Mr. Daschle lost his seat in 2004. Mr. Schumer then succeeded Mr. Reid upon his retirement and has held the post since.

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries Embraces Medicare Expansion on Eve of Speaker Vote
item.description:
Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the top House Democrat, on Tuesday endorsed a broad expansion of Medicare to cover more Americans and a wider range of services, edging closer to the Medicare for All proposal championed by progressives on the eve of his nomination to be speaker in the next Congress.

“We should lower the age of Medicare eligibility,” Mr. Jeffries said at a news conference at the Capitol, less than 24 hours before Democrats were set to gather behind closed doors for a leadership election in which he is expected to be chosen for the top post. “We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing and dental. And we should cover all the kids in the United States of America.”

The sweeping expansion outlined by Mr. Jeffries — which would cost hundreds of billions of dollars — was in line with a proposal that Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent in line to be chairman of the health committee, wants to take up next year and fast-track through Congress on a filibuster-proof bill.

Mr. Sanders and other progressives have been pushing a slow phase-in of Medicare for All that would include first lowering the eligibility age to 55, covering all children and expanding coverage for dental, vision and hearing services. Those are steps that some moderate candidates also campaigned on during midterm elections in which Democrats in both liberal bastions and conservative-leaning areas embraced economic populism.

Before the election, Mr. Jeffries did not endorse the plan. He promised only that a Democratic majority would quickly work to reverse the Medicaid cuts that were included in President Trump’s sweeping domestic policy agenda and restore Affordable Care Act tax credits that Republicans had allowed to expire.

But with a larger majority giving him more room to maneuver and progressives pressing him to take up a bolder agenda, Mr. Jeffries appears to be taking a more ambitious approach. On Tuesday, he framed the new priorities as “important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage.”

The announcement came the same day Mr. Jeffries was set to attend a Congressional Progressive Caucus board meeting, where some members have been pressing him to embrace Medicare for All before committing their support for him as speaker.

With no one stepping forward to challenge him and broad support in the caucus already wrapped up, Mr. Jeffries is expected to be nominated easily on Wednesday morning in the election by secret ballot.

Representative Greg Casar of Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus who has said he plans to vote for Mr. Jeffries, endorsed the new health care push, saying that “step by step, we will march toward health care as a human right and replace our broken, profit-driven system.”

The position is also broadly popular with Democrats across the ideological spectrum. That is where Mr. Jeffries, who likes to host listening sessions and have a caucus “family discussion” before telegraphing his stance on any issue, likes to land.

Democratic candidates who successfully flipped red districts, including Representatives-elect Bob Brooks of Pennsylvania, Randy Villegas of California and Brian Poindexter of Ohio, all ran on supporting Medicare for All, or a phased-in approach like the one Mr. Jeffries outlined on Tuesday.

Even some of the most conservative Democrats in Congress said they were on board with passing pieces of Medicare for All, even if they said they did not want to vote on the proposal itself, which is estimated to cost tens of trillions of dollars over a decade.

“Moderates have to realize we have to deliver bold results to help people with affordability,” Representative Jared Moskowitz, a centrist Democrat from Florida, said in an interview. “The progressives need to realize that their stuff doesn’t have 60 votes and the president won’t sign it. But there are components of some of their stuff we can pass and put on his desk. That’s how we’re going to have to make the sausage, but the point isn’t to pass messaging bills.”

One of the proposals that Mr. Jeffries is considering, which would add coverage for children, is a bill by Senator Andy Kim, Democrat of New Jersey. It would automatically enroll all children born in the United States into an extension of Medicaid, offering them coverage until the age of 26. Other proposals are being considered as well.

Margot Sanger-Katz contributed reporting.

item.title: Markwayne Mullin Defends Flight to L.S.U.-Texas Game After Ground Stop
item.description:
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, on Tuesday defended his decision to use a government plane to fly to a football game over the weekend as airports were still crowded following a nationwide ground stop.

Mr. Mullin traveled to Baton Rouge, La., on Saturday to see the Louisiana State University Tigers play the University of Texas Longhorns just 21 hours after the federal government lifted the ground stop, which halted flights for more than four hours beginning Friday afternoon.

“I would have never taken airspace if the airspace wasn’t open,” Mr. Mullin said on Tuesday in an interview with CNBC. “We still gotta live our lives at the same time.”

Mr. Mullin, who was initially tasked with helping to oversee the administration’s response to the ground stop, drew scrutiny after The New York Post reported that he had taken the government plane to the game while many Americans were dealing with canceled or delayed flights. Disruptions continued for days as airlines rebooked passengers and repositioned planes.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Mr. Mullin “abides by all ethics requirements” and is required by law to travel on government airplanes.

“This is to ensure access to secure communications and to comply by his constitutional duty of continuity of government should a national emergency arise,” the statement said. “Any flight not related to his service as D.H.S. secretary, he pays for personally.”

The homeland security secretary told CNBC on Tuesday that he had called Representative Steve Scalise, Republican of Louisiana, to ask for help getting the football tickets, which he said he had paid for himself. Mr. Mullin, who is from Oklahoma and represented the state in the Senate, said he attended the game because his 12-year-old great-niece was a “huge L.S.U. fan.”

The day before the game, Mr. Mullin was at the center of the Trump administration’s efforts to explain why the government had issued the ground stop. Shortly after it was announced, Mr. Mullin told reporters outside the White House that the halt was necessary because of a “telecommunication outage,” but that there was no evidence of a nefarious attack.

He held a briefing with Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, later in the day to explain that the problem had appeared to arise from an upgrade of the Federal Aviation Administration’s system. Mr. Duffy said over the weekend that the problems began after a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark., appeared to overload the system.
