item.title: F.A.A. Shelves Routers Like the One Linked to the Nationwide Ground Stop
item.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration has suspended its installation of routers like the one that transportation officials said they believed had contributed to a nationwide ground stop on Friday after it overloaded communications systems used by air traffic controllers and pilots.

The F.A.A. also disabled more than 60 other identical devices on its network after the disruptions wreaked havoc on air travel, according to the agency, which said on Tuesday that the changes had taken effect in quick succession in response to the chain of events on Friday.

Made by Juniper Networks, which was acquired last year by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, the routers were intended to replace older Cisco Systems models as part of a sweeping program by the F.A.A. to modernize its equipment.

For decades, copper wiring has been the backbone of that antiquated system, which the federal government has slowly started to replace with modern fiber-optic cables.

But while an engineer was installing one of the replacement routers on Friday at an F.A.A. radio center in El Dorado, Ark., data began flooding the network, overwhelming the system and hampering communications, federal officials said. That engineer was working for L3Harris, the company that owns the network used by the F.A.A., and was being monitored by an F.A.A. technician, officials said.

A second router at an F.A.A. radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, also became unstable, according to the F.A.A., which said technicians had resolved the problem by disabling both routers.

“So we thought it’s only prudent to pause the use of these routers,” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said at a news conference on Tuesday on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Duffy suggested the router glitch was isolated, saying that federal officials had grounded flights out of an abundance of caution.

“Sixty-eight times it worked well,” he said earlier in the news conference. “This one router started to broadcast into our network, and it started to overload the network.”

Federal transportation officials said on Tuesday that the replacement routers had been tested for a year before being installed.

“We don’t know the fault trigger,” Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, said at the news conference. “We do know that this router could be enabled to do what it did.”

In a statement on Tuesday, Adam Bauer, a spokesman for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, disputed that the Juniper Networks device was defective.

“Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured,” Mr. Bauer said. “The F.A.A. is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause.”

On Monday, Democratic members of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee sent a letter to Mr. Duffy and Mr. Bedford urging them to pause the use of the Juniper Networks routers.

“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed,” the senators wrote. “F.A.A. must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.”

On Tuesday, federal officials were less measured in their assessment of the performance of L3Harris, which Mr. Duffy said had held contracts with the F.A.A. for more than 20 years and was responsible for monitoring the network.

“They didn’t identify and isolate,” he said. “That concerns me. We have to have them perform better.”

A representative for L3Harris on Tuesday referred to a previous statement, which said the company was “supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation.”

While Mr. Duffy said there was no evidence that the system had been hacked, he noted that F.B.I. analysts were examining the router from the F.A.A. radio facility in Arkansas.

Mr. Bedford said that air traffic controllers had never lost contact with planes while the network was experiencing disruptions. He added that the F.A.A. had backup systems in place but that safety was paramount.

“And people can fly with confidence,” he said.

item.title: A National Meltdown With Nobody Manning the Help Desk
item.description:
In five short days, Americans have begun to wonder if their country is actually breaking.

It started Thursday, with the Microsoft outage. Then, on Friday, came the nationwide flight stoppage, only the third this century. After that, four major U.S. banks reported tech problems on Monday, the same day United Airlines’ computers went down. On Tuesday morning, the National Security Agency’s internal communications network was offline, then Apple services were disrupted.

The cascading series of tech failures left Americans stranded in airports, refreshing their work computers, and generally scratching their heads over what was actually happening. Was some massive hack causing a near-simultaneous shutdown of our digital arteries? Were rogue A.I. agents at work? Or was it more about the aging bones of a 20th century nation unready for the 21st, where one router and a few copper wires in Arkansas could cause everything to go kerflooey?

Perhaps most importantly, was anyone at the helm to fix it?

“I think we ought to be briefed thoroughly on what is actually happening here,” Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, told reporters Tuesday on Capitol Hill.

“If this is all a coincidence,” he added, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.”

So far, no evidence has emerged to tie the outages together. President Trump, speaking during a trip to Asia, shrugged it off, remarking, “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like this happen. It’s fine.”

But at a base level, many people were left with a feeling that the country was off-kilter. No less than Karoline Leavitt, President Trump’s uber-loyal former press secretary, was on Fox News “wondering the same thing: what’s happening?”

When the president returns from Asia, she said, “there should be a message directly to the American people, whether it’s from him or somebody else at the White House, saying what they know.”

Peter Avery’s Thursday started uneventfully — on a conference call in his company’s Irvine, Calif., office. Mid-call, co-workers and clients began texting him about not being able to login to Microsoft programs. For Mr. Avery, 57, the chief information and security officer for a cybersecurity firm, Velocity Security/Circle MSP, the event was in his wheelhouse.

“My brain goes to cyber,” he said. “I don’t jump to that conclusion, but it’s in the back of my mind.”

He said he was surprised with the sheer scale of the outage, but he boarded a flight on Friday morning for Michigan anyway. When the pilot announced the ground stop, and other passengers found out he worked in cybersecurity, he became the most popular person on the flight. Passengers peppered him with questions, and drew a parallel with the national groundstop after the attacks on 9/11.

“They were talking through pattern recognition, like humans do, trying to make sense of it,” he said.

An hour and a half later, he deplaned and waited for information at a John Wayne Airport bar, drinking an old-fashioned and getting to know his fellow passengers. The mood, he said, was oddly light. The digital debacle had brought about an analogue response — thousands of strangers rolling their eyes together and sharing travel war stories.

“It’s almost like when you have a blizzard and you get stuck with each other, and next thing you know you are playing cards and laughing,” he said.

For Jennifer Fitzpatrick, 42, a travel agency owner from Sebastian, Fla., that was almost exactly what happened. At the airport in Charlotte, N.C. on Friday night, she and a cluster of passengers she had been with for hours made up a holiday-infused tale they called “FAA-la-la. A groundstop story.”

Slightly punchy after an all-night flight from Poland, where she had been at a travel conference, she imagined an entire movie with her fellow castaways that began with them driving away in one of the airport vans that they could see from their gate, B5. (All the rental cars had been taken by then, she said.)

“We were like, ‘Listen, there’s a van down there, we could take it and just go!’” she said.

They began imagining subplots with other, unknowing passengers.

“There was a guy who kind of looked like Santa, and we wrote him into the story too,” she said.

Ms. Fitzpatrick said she heard people talking about how the stoppage could be related to the Microsoft outage, or even to the Nvidia upheaval. She didn’t believe it.

“I’m like, ‘Listen, it’s probably someone who unplugged something somewhere,’” she said, noting that, as a professional in the travel industry, hers was a fairly educated guess.

The more likely culprit, she said, were Trump administration budget cuts.

“It’s kind of like a domino ripple effect,” she said. “We are cutting so much that we are not taking care of what needs to be taken care of.”

The president, standing next to the leaders of Japan, India, and Australia at a press event in Manila, was asked if he’d spoken to the banks that had experienced outages on Monday.

“It’s going to be very much under control,” he said.

Americans disagreed — and voted with their feet.

Jenni Turner, a 58-year-old employee benefits professional had just boarded a connecting flight to her hometown, Dayton, Ohio, from Chicago on Monday when United suffered what it called a “widespread system outage.” After sitting on the plane for about an hour, the airline allowed passengers to deplane, which she did because she was scared.

“I just have the heebie-jeebies,” she said, adding, “Between Microsoft, the airlines and the banks, I think they are all connected, you cannot tell me otherwise.”

This was her second business trip this month, she said, and she will not fly again for the rest of the year: “The trust is broken.”

For Ryan Mack, the trust was never there to begin with. Mr. Mack, who works for a financial literacy nonprofit and lives in Jersey City, N.J., said he did not trust Mr. Trump as a leader, and had a sneaking suspicion that the outages may have been the result of Mr. Trump’s wheeling and dealing.

“I don’t think it’s above Trump to sell access to anything,” said Mr. Mack, 49.

“If they’re putting up war plans on Signal,” he said, referring to a misfired message to the editor of The Atlantic Magazine last year, “then what about our access to control systems? There’s nobody watching the hen house anymore.”

For some Americans, the timing and scale of the outages made sheer coincidence too hard to believe as an explanation.

“I don’t buy any conspiracy theories too much, but when something walks like a duck, looks like a duck, quacks like a duck, it’s probably a dang duck,” said Rockey Burgess, 51, the mayor of Williamston, S.C., a small town outside of Greenville.

“Maybe there’s something bigger coming,” he said, “and maybe it’s related to some of the conflicts we’re in across the world.”

Mr. Burgess, who also operates a communications equipment business, said the country used to have the “latest and greatest” infrastructure.

But now, those systems have aged, and they are no match for the “A.I. bots and other things that could literally take the place of 10,000 people trying to write code to hack into a system,” he said.

“We know China, we know Iran, both of those two wish to do us harm,” he said.

Mr. Avery, the cybersecurity expert in Michigan, was skeptical that the events over the past five days were connected.

“I like facts,” he said. “And until now, these are all separate issues.”

Drawing patterns where they do not yet exist, he said, is human nature, part of the need to make sense of things. But it can lead down a dark road.

“When you start to live in that world where everyone’s a liar and no one is telling the truth, you are starting to live in fear.”

Robert Chiarito contributed reporting from Chicago.

item.title: White House Withdraws Nomination of Heidi Overton to Be F.D.A. Commissioner
item.description:
The White House has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to be commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, on the eve of a crucial vote on her confirmation by a Senate panel, according to two people familiar with the decision.

Dr. Overton, a White House domestic policy adviser who has been involved in developing some of the administration’s most controversial health policies, would have needed every Republican vote on the Senate health committee to advance her nomination to the Senate floor. It became clear on Tuesday night that she did not have enough votes.

The decision to withdraw her nomination was first reported by Axios.

The panel’s chairman, Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, had expressed reservations about Dr. Overton from the start, saying her role in an executive order this summer that called for reducing the number of vaccines recommended for children was “almost disqualifying.” During her confirmation hearing in September, Mr. Cassidy, a physician, had pressed her repeatedly on whether she would stand up to President Trump on vaccines, particularly the measles vaccine. Dr. Overton said: “It is safe and effective and it is our best tool right now in the public health response to the measles outbreak.”

As lawmakers broached other topics, though, Dr. Overton made it clear during the hearing that she would be loyal to the president, defending his forays into decisions typically made by career scientists. “The president’s interest is in the best outcomes for the American people,” she said.

Abortion was also an issue for lawmakers of both parties. Democrats were alarmed by Dr. Overton’s past statements on the abortion pill mifepristone, which she previously called “dangerous to women.” During her confirmation hearing, Dr. Overton said that “the drug is safe and effective as labeled today” under F.D.A. regulations.

Republican were concerned that in the hearing she gave only vague answers on how she would handle a safety review of mifepristone that is underway at the agency.

The F.D.A. regulates products that account of about 20 percent of spending in the United States, including over-the-counter and prescription medications, most food, dietary supplements, cosmetics and medical devices.

It is unclear if the White House will choose another nominee as the window to confirm an F.D.A. commissioner with a Republican-led Senate is narrowing. The odds of getting a nominee confirmed once the Democrats take control of the Senate in January could be slim.

Before joining the White House during the second Trump Administration, Dr. Overton was a chief policy officer at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank. She has written articles that denounced abortion as “corrosive” to women and called for more controls over prescribing abortion pills.

When Mr. Trump announced in a social media post in August that Dr. Overton would be nominated, he said he needed her at the F.D.A. to secure the nation’s role as “the WORLD LEADER for Scientific Discovery and CURES.” He also said he expected her to deliver on his priorities, including clinical trial reforms and lower drug prices.

Jonathan Swan contributed reporting.

item.title: A.I. Mistook a Bag of Chips for a Gun, Teenagers’ Lawsuit Says
item.description:
Four current and former students of a high school in Baltimore said in a lawsuit filed on Tuesday that their civil rights had been violated when an artificial intelligence surveillance system alerted the police to a gun that was actually a bag of chips.

The students had been waiting for a ride home from football practice at Kenwood High School on Oct. 20, 2025. One of them was eating Cool Ranch Doritos, a snack from their coach, the lawsuit said.

Suddenly, police officers arrived with guns drawn and ordered the teenagers, who are Black, to their knees, handcuffed them and searched them, the lawsuit said.

“The encounter was terrifying and life-threatening,” the lawsuit said. “With armed police encircling them for no apparent reason, each student feared for his life and the lives of his friends.”

The teenagers are suing Omnilert, an A.I. gun-detection technology company; Baltimore County and its police department; and Baltimore County Public Schools. Representatives for the company and the government agencies didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment on Tuesday evening.

After the episode, the school district and the police said in a statement that both agencies were “committed to taking additional steps to ensure all staff fully understand and follow established protocols to prevent such incidents from occurring again.”

The surveillance system scans security footage for firearms, the lawsuit said. Through a camera near where the teenagers were standing, Omnilert mistook the chips for a gun.

A school resource officer and the principal later made light of the ordeal, with texts using emojis, the lawsuit said.

“It was a bag of chips,” the principal, Catherine Smith, texted to administrators using four emojis crying from laughter, according to the lawsuit.

The Maryland Office of the Inspector General for Education investigated the episode, found no evidence of racial bias and said the A.I. system had detected the hand position of one of the teenagers while holding an item as a potential threat, WMAR-TV reported.

The report highlighted system flaws, including that the principal had not seen a cancellation notice from other school staff members and had contacted the police, the TV station reported.

One of the teenagers is a current student and the three others are now in college, the lawsuit said.

Their constitutional rights to protecting due process and their right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures were violated, the lawsuit said.

By suing, the teenagers and their families want recognition from the police, the school and the company that what happened to them was unacceptable, said Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, a nonprofit legal organization representing them.

The teenagers also want school officials and the police to enact protocols to prevent false alerts from triggering armed police responses, he said.

All the officers had photos of one of the boys holding a bag of chips, Mr. Kamdang said, adding, “This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed A.I. to substitute for their judgment.”

One of the officers later told the teenagers that it was a good thing they had not run, underscoring the dangers Black people face during interactions with law enforcement officers, Mr. Kamdang said.

“For anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation,” he said. “For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life or death situation.”

item.title: Mary Peltola Flips Alaska Senate Seat for Democrats
item.description:
Mary Peltola, an Alaska Democrat and former congresswoman, flipped a hotly contested Senate seat, The Associated Press said on Tuesday, ousting the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, in a reliably conservative state.

The result punctuated Democrats’ strong performance nationwide and added to the party’s new majority in the Senate.

Ms. Peltola, who in 2022 became the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress, will now become the first Democrat to represent the state in the Senate since 2015. Campaigning in a rural state that historically votes for Republicans for president, she began the race as an underdog against Senator Sullivan, a two-term incumbent who had forged deep relationships with various constituencies.

But Ms. Peltola capitalized on the intense frustration among Alaskans about the state’s high cost of living, especially the skyrocketing price of fuel, which many voters blamed on President Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran. Affordability concerns were magnified in Alaska, where goods from the contiguous United States are strikingly expensive and gas prices reached $8 per gallon or higher in rural parts of the state.

A former state legislator and commercial fisher, Ms. Peltola ran a cautious campaign that strained to avoid ties with the national Democratic Party. She never deviated from her longstanding slogan: “Fish, Family, Freedom.” She also weathered a major staff shake-up in August and a scandal in September, when The New York Times reported that she had mistreated and verbally abused her staff over the years. At the time, Ms. Peltola’s campaign said some of the accusations were exaggerated or false.

Despite significant attention paid to the presence of two other candidates on Alaska’s four-person ranked-choice ballot, their presence may not have had much of an effect on the final outcome of the race.

One of those candidates was named Dan J. Sullivan, a twist in the campaign that Republicans had argued for months was a Democratic plot to confuse voters and aid Ms. Peltola. They tried unsuccessfully to remove Dan J. Sullivan, a retiree from a small fishing village, from the ballot, and Mr. Trump’s Justice Department sued ahead of the election in a pre-emptive effort to invalidate the result.

In October, The Times reported that national Democrats and aides for Ms. Peltola had indeed worked to recruit other candidates onto the ballot, including Dan J. Sullivan. That finding fueled Republican efforts to discredit Ms. Peltola, even though The Times found no evidence of illegal activity. Ms. Peltola has denied knowing about the plan to stack the ballot, contrary to an assertion by her former campaign manager, who said she was aware.

Throughout the campaign, Senator Sullivan was placed in the unenviable position of having to defend an unpopular administration and justify high prices. At campaign stops with Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance, the senator acknowledged that Alaskans were hurting, but tried to blame voters’ woes on Democrats. He also argued that Democrats would stop oil drilling projects that drive the state’s economy if they regained control of the Senate.

item.title: Trump Administration Presses Ahead in Legal Battle Over U.S. Attorneys
item.description:
The Justice Department said in a filing late Tuesday that it would challenge the latest court ruling to threaten the standing of President Trump’s favored U.S. attorneys.

The new filing, in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, signaled a continuation of efforts by the Trump administration to leave interim prosecutors in place instead of appointing permanent U.S. attorneys who require Senate confirmation.

The latest U.S. attorney under scrutiny is Bill Essayli, who was sworn in April 2025 as the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles. On Monday, Judge J. Michael Seabright of the Federal District Court in Hawaii refused to stay an earlier ruling that disqualified Mr. Essayli from overseeing two pending criminal cases because he was serving unlawfully.

In response, the Justice Department said in its filing that it planned to “seek emergency relief.”

Permanent U.S. attorney appointments typically require approval either by the U.S. Senate or by federal judges in the affected district. But Mr. Essayli was among a group of Trump allies who were initially appointed “interim” U.S. attorneys last year. Interim appointments expire after 120 days. After the appointments expired, the administration designated them first assistant U.S. attorneys and kept them in place running their offices on an acting basis.

The practice quickly faced legal tests, leading a variety of federal judges to reject the strategy.

Ultimately, the United States Supreme Court could decide the matter, perhaps as soon as this winter. The high court is already weighing whether to intervene in parallel cases involving the tenuous status of two other top prosecutors: Sigal Chattah in Nevada and John A. Sarcone III in the Northern District of New York. Any decision by the court in those cases, if it does intervene, would affect a range of prosecutors, including Mr. Essayli.

In a separate filing on Tuesday, in the case involving Ms. Chattah, government lawyers said the lower court decision leading to her disqualification “risks chaos during future presidential transitions and casts a pall over roughly a dozen U.S. Attorney’s Offices nationwide.”

The Department of Justice had no immediate comment on Tuesday.

The president has named a number of his closest allies as top federal prosecutors, some of whom lack any prosecutorial experience. Mr. Essayli is a former Republican lawmaker from California, and Ms. Chattah was the Republican candidate for Nevada attorney general in 2022. Mr. Sarcone has pursued investigations of Letitia James, the New York State attorney general, who has been a frequent target of the president’s ire.

One of the most unusual legal clashes has come in Seattle, where federal judges appointed Roger Rogoff, only for him to be fired by the administration less than an hour after his appointment. Mr. Rogoff filed a lawsuit contesting his termination, was briefly reinstated, and was then removed again pending a stay. Charles Neil Floyd, a former immigration judge installed by the Trump administration, has been running the office on an acting basis.

Anne Joseph O’Connell, a professor at Stanford University Law School, said a resolution could come soon, noting that petitions were pending on the Supreme Court calendar “for the Justices to discuss in early December.” How the issue is resolved, she added, could decide whether future presidents can get around Senate confirmations for a variety of offices, not just prosecutors.

item.title: U.S. Bishops Seek to Engage A.I. Companies on Moral Issues
item.description:
At the urging of Pope Leo XIV, America’s Roman Catholic bishops are making the scrutiny of artificial intelligence a top political and pastoral priority, even as they continue to speak out on concerns like the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

Vatican officials have pushed American bishops to take a leading role on the issue in recent months, as many of the most powerful A.I. companies in the world are based in the United States. This week, the bishops are discussing the topic at their annual fall meeting in Baltimore, though they at times struggle to navigate the fast-evolving technology.

Their agenda so far involves engaging business leaders and government officials on A.I. regulation, as well as educating church leaders around the country on the technology itself. The bishops hope to address the negative impact A.I. may have on workers, families and the environment, and to understand how it may exacerbate existing challenges like global poverty and migration.

“This concerted effort on the part of the church in the U.S. to engage is of supreme importance,” Cardinal Michael Czerny, who leads a new Vatican commission on A.I. that Leo established this year, said in an interview. “Theirs is the flagship role by accident of history and geography.”

The American bishops recently created their own A.I. task force, led by Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, Calif., whose diocese includes much of Silicon Valley. Warnings about A.I.’s potentially dangerous capabilities — even the possibility of human extinction — have added urgency to the mission.

The new group, which includes eight bishops and three academic consultants, met in person for the first time on Sunday and is still sorting out specifics of the bishops’ upcoming state and federal advocacy. Bishop Cantú said the task force is especially concerned about A.I.’s impact on human dignity and work, the safety and education of children, the security of banking institutions, and Catholic health care systems.

On policy issues like abortion and immigration, the bishops have long taken their concerns to the government. But with A.I., they are also positioning themselves as diplomats to technology leaders, representing Catholic moral priorities.

“This situation is different from the immigration or the abortion issue, because to some degree those are clearer and we know what is at stake,” Bishop Cantú said in an interview. “We are trying to understand the technology and what we need to advocate for.”

The bishops’ fall meeting is their second major gathering since Leo issued his teaching about A.I.’s risk to humans this spring. When they met last fall, the bishops issued an unusual, near-unanimous statement rebuking the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement tactics. In past meetings, topics like whether politicians who support reproductive rights should be denied communion have prompted colorful floor debates.

But A.I. presents unique challenges for the bishops. The technology is foreign to many of them. An older and more formal cohort, some bishops rarely even send text messages, preferring older styles of communication and work.

“We are still getting our sea legs,” Bishop Cantú said. “I joke with my brother bishops that I’ve got my cape, and we’re going to save humanity in the next three years.”

As an institution, the Catholic Church also tends not to move quickly, a reality at odds with the urgency many of the bishops feel.

“The church thinks in centuries,” Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone of San Francisco said. “A.I., one month is centuries.”

Archbishop Cordileone said he felt a special responsibility given his region, which is home to technology companies with tremendous power. Anthropic, a leading A.I. company located in his archdiocese, is expected to begin selling its stock to the public this week with a valuation of more than $1 trillion.

“People with that much power can only use it well, for the good of humanity, if they are virtuous,” Archbishop Cordileone said. “They need to be humble, patient, generous, and have a sense of compassion and solidarity, especially with those who are needy. Our role is to help them be aware of this.”

The bishops’ new task force does not report to the Vatican’s A.I. commission. The latter, which is also just taking shape, can be a resource to help local bishops as they interact with A.I. companies, Cardinal Blase Cupich of Chicago said. In particular, the U.S. bishops are looking to offer insights to the companies about the pope’s moral teachings, including on protecting human dignity.

“Our job is to keep in contact with them, be of service to them but to be very clear what their moral responsibility is,” Cardinal Cupich, a member of the bishops’ A.I. task force, said.

The task force came together after a small group of bishops, including Cardinal Cupich, Archbishop Cordileone and Bishop Cantú, visited Silicon Valley in August and met with leaders of Anthropic, Google and Meta.

In those meetings, the bishops also raised concerns on behalf of the global church, since the choices of American companies affect families across the world. In one conversation, Cardinal Cupich said, leaders of one A.I. company suggested they would be open to new tax policies that would leverage their revenues to help support people who lose their jobs because of A.I. (He declined to name which company.)

“What about those countries that don’t have access to tax revenues?” Cardinal Cupich said. “This could really blow up, with more people trying to escape poverty created by job displacement in their countries.”

Catholic bishops in other parts of the world are also trying to find ways to adopt the principles of Leo’s encyclical. Last month in Brussels, a delegation representing the Catholic bishops of the European Union offered a set of A.I. guidelines to the E.U., urging it to be a leader in international governance and regulation. Catholic bishops representing Asia plan to promote A.I. literacy and expand what they see as missionary work with “digital creators.”

In the United States, the bishops’ task force plans to develop internal guidelines on how Catholic entities should use A.I. It is also is planning a series of webinars with technology engineers, first for bishops, then other church leaders and parishes, to educate them on the technology itself.

Leaders at the bishops’ conference have already met with engineers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google, as well as METR, a nonprofit A.I. organization, Bishop Cantú said.

He also said he understood that the companies have their own agendas beyond the church’s moral goals. Anthropic, for example, engaged in a private, yearlong effort to court religious thinkers and persuade them to accept the company’s views of its computer systems — even the possibility that Claude, its flagship product, might be conscious. (Leo has made clear that Catholic teaching does not allow for machine consciousness.)

At a news conference on Tuesday, Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, urged humans not to abdicate responsibility to AI. “We are the deciders,” he said. “It is ours to guide and direct.”

Beyond the policy considerations, the bishops are looking for ways to make sure their parishioners understand the church’s positions on A.I., especially Pope Leo’s aim of protecting human dignity and agency.

From Rome, Cardinal Czerny has urged the U.S. bishops to take seriously what the people in their pews are experiencing as A.I. changes the world around them.

“We think that the hostility toward the data centers is a way of expressing much broader and deeper anxieties,” Cardinal Czerny said. “Who is listening to those folks? We think it is very important that the church listen.”

item.title: Fans Flock to This Famous Sign. Neighbors Say, Get Off My Road.
item.description:
The Hollywood sign is an irresistible attraction to tourists and Californians alike, but it’s created a traffic nightmare in the wealthy neighborhoods just below it.

And that has spurred local residents into action, trying to impose some order on an unruly jumble of vehicles seeking the best viewing spots.

“You can’t park in the red and you can’t park on this side of the street,” yelled Lisa Hope, who lives nearby in the Hollywood Hills, admonishing a driver who parked in the fire lane facing oncoming traffic.

That driver moved away, but Ms. Hope was fighting a losing battle against the unrelenting parade of vehicles fixing to do the same.

On a recent Friday, cars and vans clogged the narrow, serpentine roads that connect the multimillion-dollar homes in the Hollywood Hills. Traffic was at a standstill on a sharp incline adjacent to Lake Hollywood Park. The imminent risk of collision seemed to lurk at the many hairpin turns on the way up to the sweeping views of the sign and the city of Los Angeles below.

Few, if any, Los Angeles landmarks carry the allure of the nine, 45-foot high white letters that stand atop the Hollywood Hills — and few neighborhoods could be less suited to accommodate the crowds that turn out in force to see them.

And as civic disputes go, few highlight the intersection of moneyed privilege and public access so vividly.

The tourist-driven disorder is not new, but the increased threat of wildfires in recent years has alarmed the people living nearby. Late last month, a group of them sued the city of Los Angeles, accusing it of failing to adequately address complaints going back years about the dangers posed by hordes of sightseers and their vehicles. The suit claims that the city has encouraged the mayhem.

The lawsuit does not seek damages. Instead, it asks a judge to force the city to find a way to stem the grinding traffic in the hills and put an end to the illicit activity that comes with the high volume of tourists. Otherwise, the plaintiffs say, the crush of cars and blatant parking violations will present a dangerous obstacle to firefighters seeking access to a blaze roaring through the hills, or to local residents trying to evacuate.

They also cite the many cigarette butts that visitors have dropped as a serious fire risk.

“No one is seeking to prevent tourists from seeing the Hollywood sign, this truly iconic, historic landmark,” said Ilan Wurman, the lawyer representing the plaintiffs. “But the neighbors are entitled to a clean and safe and healthful environment in the public spaces of their neighborhood, as any neighborhood is, and we believe the city can accomplish both things.”

Absent help from the city, Ms. Hope and two of her neighbors, Marissa Allen Cohen and Cindy Cobb, tried to take matters into their own hands on the recent afternoon.

The trio took stock of the scene: a line of cars parked in a fire lane; a handful of street vendors selling fruit, coffee and souvenirs; people descending into the foliage of a ditch to relieve themselves; and a man lighting up a cigarette not far from a no smoking sign featuring Smokey Bear.

“There’s no smoking,” Ms. Hope hollered at the man. He nodded and offered an apologetic smirk before putting out the cigarette.

“Some people just go, ‘I don’t care,’” Ms. Hope said.

Over the summer, Ms. Cobb and her neighbors helped raise money to hire Mr. Wurman, whose firm had successfully secured judgments against other cities over their management of public spaces.

In Phoenix, for example, Mr. Wurman’s firm successfully argued that the city was liable for mitigating any public nuisances created by a third party on property owned by the city. It persuaded a judge to order Phoenix to clear a large homeless encampment that had taken over a neighborhood.

The lawsuit against Los Angeles claims that the city has had a direct hand in encouraging the increase in tourists in the neighborhood. It points to an area of brush that was cleared and graded by the City Council in 2011. The spot happened to have a perfect view of the Hollywood sign, and its location soon appeared on online maps and was labeled a viewing site.

With the advent of GPS, and the ability of social media to help publicize viewing spots, tourists knew how to get to the cleared area. Now, the lawsuit says, the cleared brush is one of the main “nuisance” sites.

In response to the lawsuit, the office of Mayor Karen Bass said that the city had already taken steps to address the traffic and safety issues, including putting more police in the area during peak visiting hours.

But the homeowners’ complaints have also raised questions about wealth and entitlement.

Angelenos reacting to local news reports on the lawsuit have derided the legal effort, saying that the homeowners put themselves in the predicament by choosing to live near a site as famous as the sign, which was constructed in 1923.

“That sign didn’t pop up yesterday, and you don’t get to close off public access to public land because you feel it’s a nuisance,” one person commented.

Melody Hernandez, who grew up and lives in Los Angeles, recently took her uncle and cousin who were visiting from Guatemala to see the sign. She was sympathetic to concerns about fire safety, but worried about an outcome in which well-off locals could effectively cut off access to a popular public place.

“I just hope their concerns are really based off their safety,” Ms. Hernandez said.

Local residents acknowledge that their complaints might seem like a special form of NIMBYism from wealthy Angelenos living in one of the toniest neighborhoods of the city. They argue that some problems are not just a nuisance, but a danger to sightseers and homeowners alike.

Ms. Cobb, a school counselor who lives around the corner from Lake Hollywood Park, says she spent thousands of dollars to fence off an area behind her home because it had become a hangout for visitors looking to smoke.

In another section of the hills, Max Martens, also a plaintiff in the suit, started uploading to YouTube videos he filmed of tense standoffs between motorists outside his home. The videos capture drivers yelling at each other, Mr. Martens and neighbors pleading with parking enforcement officers to issue tickets, and emergency vehicles such as ambulances and fire engines stalled in traffic jams.Mr. Martens and Ms. Cobb said their ultimate concern was a fire, which would threaten the lives of tourists, homeowners and street vendors equally.

“There’s people from all over the world up there that don’t know how to get out during an emergency and are dropped off by Ubers,” Ms. Cobb said. The dangers she seeks to address extend to people of all economic backgrounds, she said.

The Palisades and Eaton fires last year were a “wake-up call,” Mr. Martens said. “We are terrified of the fire danger and if we don’t do something, evacuation would be deadly.”

Ms. Cobb and other plaintiffs say they are equally concerned about the smoking.

Ms. Cobb says she has spent some weekend mornings picking up the cigarette butts she finds in her neighborhood, collecting hundreds inside a large plastic bag.

It’s up to the city to figure out how to alleviate the tourist frenzy and the risks it creates, said Mr. Wurman, the lawyer. That could include ramped-up traffic enforcement, capacity restrictions or any other number of measures, including returning the graded viewing area back to the shrubby undeveloped patch of land it was previously, he said.

The sightseers and those conducting business in the area acknowledge the problems, too.

Ricardo Guerrero, a photographer who makes his living taking photos of people in front of the sign, said that he and other photographers do their best to pick up trash and keep the viewing areas clean. The vendors making a living there — selling snacks and cold drinks — also have a stake in keeping order, he said.

Andreas Bircher, 36, who was visiting from Utah — and acknowledged that he had parked in a fire lane to snap a quick photo — said that if he were a resident, he would be frustrated, too.

But he also pointed out that there was little anyone could do about what was at the root of the problem: the enduring appeal of the sign itself.

“Unless they get rid of the sign, there’s always going to be people coming up here to try and get a picture,” Mr. Bircher said.

item.title: American A.I. Models Have Potential to Be Turned Against U.S., Study Finds
item.description:
American artificial intelligence models could help enemy extremists carry out mass-casualty events by providing attack plans and instructions on how to build explosives, according to a federal government investigation published on Wednesday.

Researchers were able to evade built-in safety restrictions in four chatbots that subsequently generated information that could be used in planning violence or attacks on the nation’s economic institutions, according to the report from the Government Accountability Office.

The study, conducted at the request of Senator Maggie Hassan, Democrat of New Hampshire, involved OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini and SpaceXAI’s Grok. Researchers did not identify which models failed or passed specific tests because they said they did not want their experiments to be re-created.

Two of the unidentified models were found to yield results helping to build or detonate an improvised explosive device, or I.E.D., for carrying out a mass-casualty event. In another test, two of the models generated information to support a plot to target the electrical grid with a drone or firearms to cause economic damage.

“Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing and attack methods,” the report said, adding that the attack plans were produced in less than 12 hours.

Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI each provided detailed comments in response to the report from the accountability office. They said that they took A.I. safety matters seriously, acknowledged that risks existed when bad actors try to bypass security restrictions and said that they had made additional improvements to prevent misuse in more recent releases of their models.The tested models were found at times to supply dates and times of when to carry out an attack, guides to maximize damage, and maps and diagrams to support a potentially violent event.The prompts triggered built-in safeguards on the A.I. platforms, including denial and account suspension. But the researchers involved in the study were able to navigate around the roadblocks with “common safeguard-bypassing techniques,” the report said. It did not clearly explain those specific techniques.

“A terrorist can log onto an A.I. platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Ms. Hassan said. The report, she added, “makes it clear that the A.I. public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”

Ms. Hassan is set to lead the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee next year, and said that one of the panel’s first hearings would examine security risks posed by A.I., including to critical infrastructure, with the goal of developing legislation. Her comments are another sign that Democrats want to take an active role in the new Congress to explore regulation of A.I. following the party’s victories in the midterm elections — in which worries about the technology ranked high for voters.

President Trump and many Republicans, however, have shown little interest in policing A.I. and have generally viewed safety concerns as overblown. Instead of creating rules for deploying and fine-tuning its models, the administration has instead largely relied on the A.I. industry to regulate itself.

The use of artificial intelligence by terrorist networks is a growing concern among U.S. security officials. The New York Times reported earlier this year on field research conducted with defectors from the extremist group Boko Haram demonstrating how A.I. tools had aided terrorist groups directly on the battlefield despite efforts by their makers to safeguard them from misuse.

In September, Anthropic released a threat report documenting attempts to use Claude to generate software for the design and development of conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs. It detailed three cases in China, two in Russia and one in Yemen.

The Government Accountability Office has a range of responsibilities that include monitoring federal spending, identifying government waste and ensuring that the executive branch complies with the wishes of Congress. Earlier this week, Mr. Trump nominated Eric M. Ueland, a top deputy at the White House budget office, to serve as the nation’s comptroller general. If confirmed, Mr. Ueland would assume control of the accountability office for a 15-year term.

item.title: House Democrats Cast Wide Net as They Prepare Trump Investigations
item.description:
House Democrats are pushing on several fronts to investigate President Trump’s administration and family and the role of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in Nvidia-related policy, as lawmakers lay the groundwork for a forceful oversight agenda when they take control of Congress next year.

Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, sent a dozen notices on Wednesday morning to members of Mr. Trump’s family, Vice President JD Vance and current and former administration officials asking them to preserve documents on a host of investigative targets.

In a separate letter on Tuesday, top Democrats on the Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees demanded that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm formerly run by Mr. Lutnick, preserve records connected to Nvidia and its business in Asia.

In their letter, Representatives Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory W. Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California said they planned to investigate whether Mr. Lutnick may have influenced the Trump administration’s rules on advanced A.I. chips and data centers to benefit Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now run by his sons, and its clients.

Taken together, the actions suggest that Democrats are casting a wide net as they push forward with plans to investigate the Trump administration, undeterred by White House threats to criminally prosecute members of Congress for carrying out their oversight responsibilities.

Since Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections this month, the White House counsel and a top Justice Department official have sent letters arguing that Democrats bent on exercising oversight of the administration risked exceeding their constitutionally derived powers and crossing “into blatant criminality,” an assessment that legal experts called dubious.

House Democrats had sent scores of letters over the past two years seeking information on potential areas of investigation, and have had no success compelling cooperation from the administration given their minority status. But the missives this week point to clear targets they plan to pursue when they take the majority in January and have the power to issue subpoenas.

Mr. Lutnick had already been a focus of Democrats. Mr. Raskin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, opened an investigation earlier this year into whether Cantor Fitzgerald improperly benefited from Mr. Lutnick’s knowledge of tariff policy, allegations that the firm denies.

More recently, Mr. Lutnick’s involvement in technology policy has been in the spotlight given the scandal surrounding former Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, who was in a relationship with a woman that U.S. intelligence agencies believed to be a Chinese spy. That woman, Alice Huang, was an executive at a Singapore-based company that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

As the fallout has grown, Mr. Lutnick has faced accusations from other Trump administration officials that he may have delayed implementing regulations that curbed the sale of Nvidia chips to Asian companies. The New York Times also reported this week that Mr. Lutnick pushed to weaken rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of Cantor Fitzgerald.

In their letter on Tuesday, addressed to Mr. Lutnick’s son Brandon, the chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald, Mr. Raskin, Mr. Meeks and Ms. Kamlager-Dove said that they were concerned Mr. Lutnick had possibly “compromised national security interests” to benefit his children and the firm they run.

“We seek to understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests,” the Democrats wrote. Mr. Raskin and Mr. Meeks are the top Democrats on the Judiciary and Foreign Affairs Committees, while Ms. Kamlager-Dove leads Democrats on a panel on South and Central Asia.

A spokeswoman for Cantor Fitzgerald said in a statement that the claims in the letter were inaccurate and that the firm’s work had not influenced government decisions.

Separately, Mr. Garcia sent letters to two of Mr. Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, asking for information related to potential conflicts of interests and allegations of corruption.

In particular, he sought information about Mr. Trump’s sons’ stake in World Liberty Financial, the family’s main cryptocurrency company; Mr. Kushner’s private equity firm, Affinity Partners; and reports that a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin paid for an after-party for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding.

Mr. Garcia also sent letters to Stephen Miller, the White House chief of staff, and Kristi Noem, the former homeland security secretary, asking them to preserve records related to what he called the “the violence, abuse, and corruption” carried out by federal immigration agents.

He also requested that Mr. Vance, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Susie Wiles, the former White House chief of staff, preserve documents related to the Trump administration’s handling of an investigation into the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein and files related to it.

“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Mr. Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans.”

item.title: Fish and High Prices: How Mary Peltola Triumphed in Alaska’s Senate Race
item.description:
In the end, Mary Peltola may not have needed two Dan Sullivans on the ballot after all.

A final batch of votes pushed Ms. Peltola, the Democratic former congresswoman, across the threshold to victory against Senator Dan S. Sullivan of Alaska late on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press. Ms. Peltola’s victory secured a 56th seat in the Senate for her party in a midterm election that Democrats swept.

She won by over 12,000 votes, more than the roughly 4,700 earned by Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whom Democratic operatives had recruited into the race in an apparent effort to confuse Republicans and siphon their votes from an incumbent with the same name.

Around the country, the presence of that other Dan Sullivan on the ballot dominated coverage of the race. But in Alaska, Ms. Peltola laid the groundwork for a dominant victory over the incumbent through more conventional means, attacking him on the cost of living and positioning herself as a working-class champion.

Like other Democrats who flipped G.O.P. seats this month, Ms. Peltola capitalized on voter anger over high gas and diesel fuel costs, the war in Iran and an unpopular president. But in Alaska, where regional matters and politicians’ personal brands play an outsize role, Ms. Peltola’s win also reflected her success running as a broadly palatable challenger steeped in local concerns. By the end, seemingly everyone knew Ms. Peltola’s campaign slogan: “Fish, Family, Freedom.”

“They had a good strategy,” said Ashley Reed, a nonpartisan state lobbyist who, like many supporters of the incumbent, begrudgingly acknowledged that Ms. Peltola’s attacks had hit home. “They just hammered away, and one of the things that worked real well is the Sullivan campaign did not counter some really harsh claims.”

While the senator focused on communities in the Mat-Su Valley and the Kenai Peninsula, conservative areas outside Anchorage, Ms. Peltola was trekking to tiny rural villages in far-flung parts of the state, many of which are reachable only by boat or small plane. She flew in and out of distant towns for days in a row, covering thousands of miles. She reached some of them by snowmobile.

“It matters who shows up,” said Gloria Burns, the president of the Ketchikan Indian Community in southeastern Alaska, who supported Ms. Peltola. “That attracted me, because I have to be thinking about who pushes for and supports policies that are best for my people.”

Ms. Peltola’s travel seemed to pay off. An analysis of voting data by district showed that the remote rural regions of Alaska shifted the most toward Democrats when compared with 2024. And although turnout was down across the board compared with the presidential election that year, the rural districts generally saw the smallest turnout declines.

Outside money and other resources flooded the state, aiding both candidates. The state’s Democratic machinery went into overdrive, with the AFL-CIO knocking on more than 28,000 doors of fellow union members, according to Bronson Frye, the group’s secretary-treasurer — far more than the roughly 10,000 the union might knock in a normal year.

From the beginning, Ms. Peltola’s allies knew that toppling a two-term incumbent would be difficult. Mr. Sullivan was seen as a low-key and relatively uncontroversial figure, and he had forged deep relationships with various constituencies in the state, including certain Alaska Native corporate interests and those working in the oil industry. The Democrats saw opportunity, however, in the senator’s understated persona, capitalizing on his struggle to differentiate himself from Mr. Trump.

“He didn’t know what to do in a campaign where the Republican brand wasn’t going to save him,” said John-Henry Heckendorn, an Alaska political strategist who worked with super PACs supporting Ms. Peltola.

Mr. Heckendorn said a moment crystallizing that struggle came in late October, when thousands arrived in Anchorage for the 60th annual Alaska Federation of Natives convention.

It was a high-profile opportunity for political candidates to sway a crucial swing bloc just before the election, and attendees were eager to watch the top two candidates face off in a forum. But Mr. Sullivan didn’t show up, giving Ms. Peltola the stage to herself to talk about how to reduce large-scale commercial fishing and bring down high costs, and to link Mr. Sullivan to Mr. Trump.

The senator had delivered a solo speech earlier at the convention. A senior adviser for his campaign disputed the idea that the decision not to appear onstage with Ms. Peltola was an unforced error. The adviser, who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe internal campaign strategy, argued instead that the national environment was the main culprit in Mr. Sullivan’s loss.

The adviser also acknowledged, however, that Democratic attacks against Mr. Sullivan, which had begun even before Ms. Peltola entered the race, appeared to have left a mark. He said Democrats’ efforts to recruit potential spoiler candidates including Daniel J. Sullivan, which were revealed in a New York Times article in October, had aided Ms. Peltola’s campaign beyond just vote tallies, by dominating news headlines and deflecting attention from her.

Mr. Sullivan did find opportunities to go on offense. He pushed Ms. Peltola to engage in more televised debates. And Ms. Peltola at times proceeded with caution, skipping chances to engage with her opponent and avoiding the national media spotlight. Mr. Sullivan derided her as “No Show Peltola.”

Still, Ms. Peltola had become well-known in Alaska after campaigning statewide three times for the House. A former commercial fisher who later served in the State Legislature, she also led a commission that served as an intermediary between Alaska Natives and outside agencies that enforced rules on fishing.

She focused heavily this year — as she always has — on her opposition to large-scale trawlers, which compete with subsistence fishers seeking to fill their freezers before Alaska’s long winters.

Ms. Peltola’s message began feeling increasingly relevant, Alaskans said, as the fishing crisis grew more acute, and as skyrocketing prices of diesel and other goods were putting the state on edge. (Mr. Sullivan also opposed trawling, focusing particularly on Russian and Chinese fleets, but he didn’t make the issue a centerpiece of his campaign.)

Four years ago, “she was a little bit alone in this critique of the way Alaska’s managing this resource,” said Joelle Hall, the former president of the Alaska AFL-CIO, the state’s largest labor union. “As time goes on, more and more people realize, ‘Oh, what’s going on?’”

Art Hackney, a veteran G.O.P. strategist in Alaska who worked for super PACs backing Mr. Sullivan, said the senator’s campaign assumed that voters knew about his legislative record, which allowed Ms. Peltola to drive a “relentlessly dishonest” narrative that he was not working to address the cost of living even as his family business had continued to make profits.

“I don’t think Dan’s campaign inoculated himself well” against the attacks, Mr. Hackney said. He added: “People just wanted to punish anyone in Trump’s realm,” and Ms. Peltola “was just riding the tide.”

Ms. Peltola was also on the defensive at times. In September, The Times reported that she had been verbally abusive to her employees, used offensive slurs and even shoved a former aide. Her campaign denied some of the allegations and said others had been exaggerated.

The next month, The Times reported that her campaign participated in an effort to recruit candidates into the Senate race, including Daniel J. Sullivan — a charge that Ms. Peltola had denied for months and continues to contest.

Republicans seized on the news, with the Justice Department suing to block certification in the event Ms. Peltola won. Mr. Trump suggest it amounted to voter fraud, though no illegal activity had been alleged.

Ms. Peltola sought to dismiss the controversies as unwanted distractions coming from the Lower 48. Even so, as the state’s round-the-clock summer sunlight gave way to snowfall in the final weeks, she remained locked in a competitive battle with Mr. Sullivan.

“I don’t think there was ever any moment where it’s like, ‘Oh yeah, we’ve got it,’” said Martha McKenna, a longtime political consultant for Ms. Peltola. “This felt like an underdog race every single day.”

By the end, Mr. Sullivan was openly acknowledging high prices in his stump speeches, and national Republicans were swooping in to help his campaign. “Too many families are having a real hard time making ends meet,” he said at an early October rally with Vice President JD Vance in Fairbanks.

Mr. Sullivan argued that Democratic control of Congress would worsen Alaska’s economic woes by squeezing the oil industry. But like many other Republicans on the ballot this year, he struggled to find a response that resonated with voters who were angry about prices in Mr. Trump’s second term. Unlike some Republican lawmakers who voted for a resolution to curtail the president’s ability to continue to the war with Iran, which drove up oil prices, Mr. Sullivan largely supported the president on the conflict.

For more than a year, Ms. Hall, a Peltola ally, had worried that the president would show up and deliver an October surprise that could give Mr. Sullivan a final boost. Mr. Trump did just that, announcing at a rally in Wasilla last month that South Korea would invest $54 billion in a long-delayed natural gas pipeline in the state.

But as Ms. Hall saw it, Mr. Trump’s credibility had become so damaged that voters weren’t interested.

“By that point, Alaskans were like, ‘You know what, this guy’s full of it,” she said.

On election night, as the Democratic landslide swept many of his Republican colleagues out of office, Mr. Sullivan predicted that his state would defy the trend.

Two weeks later, he was swept out, too.

Christine Zhang contributed reporting.

item.title: This Town Revolted Against Amazon’s ‘Drone Highway’
item.description:
In a font that begged for a magnifying glass, right below the newspaper’s classified ads, there it was: Notice of Public Hearing.

Christine Farmer, a longtime resident of Westborough, Mass., normally skipped over legal notices in the weekly Community Advocate, but she caught it by chance — a public hearing in mid-September on Amazon’s request to build a staging area and launch zones for its new drone delivery service. The project would be based at the company’s warehouse less than two miles from Ms. Farmer’s home.

It was the first time Ms. Farmer, a 63-year-old executive coach and business consultant, had heard about plans for drone deliveries in the region.

Like many of her neighbors in Westborough, Ms. Farmer loved Amazon. A few months earlier, she had nearly hugged an Amazon driver to thank him for bringing her a package — by electric van — that she needed that same day.

But the drone deliveries felt startling and unnecessary, she thought — an existential change.

Were delivery drones really something Westborough needed, zipping over its ponds and parks, hiking trails and tall, tall trees?

Ms. Farmer’s decision to attend the meeting eventually led her to a place she never expected to be: in the thick of a growing rebellion against Amazon and its plans for drone delivery dominance across America.

In 2013, Amazon introduced the concept of widespread drone delivery as if it was a fait accompli, with its founder, Jeff Bezos, saying that it “will work, and it will happen.” The reason for it was simple, the company has said: customers demand ever faster service.

Amazon now has 20 drone hubs, and in August, and the company said that it aimed to expand drone deliveries to nearly 500 U.S. towns and cities, including more than 60 hubs, by the end of the year. Some local governments have readily approved the company’s plans.

“As residents learn more about it and see it for themselves, Prime Air is a welcome addition to communities,” said Lindsay Hamilton, an Amazon spokeswoman, adding that the drone program reduces traffic on the road and brings highly skilled jobs.

But some residents, like Ms. Farmer, are dreading an influx of 83-pound flying machines that seem straight out of “The Jetsons.” Zooming across the sky at up to 74 miles an hour, they look to some residents like colossal interplanetary insects and sound like a supersized swarm of locusts.

Opponents of the drones are fuming at the Federal Aviation Administration for ruling that commercial delivery drones would not significantly affect “the human environment” and that each location did not need a full environmental review. (The F.A.A. declined to comment.) And they are furious with local authorities for not doing more to push back against the impending changes to the sights and sounds of everyday life.

If Amazon drones come, Ms. Farmer asked, what would stop Walmart drones from following? Or DoorDash? Target? Home Depot?

“We will be living under a drone highway, and who would want that?” said Ms. Farmer, who raised two daughters in Westborough, a town of about 23,000 people, 30 miles west of Boston.

She continued, “I really just can’t imagine living in a world where the skies just aren’t quiet anymore.”

Before the Westborough planning board meeting in mid-September, Ms. Farmer went out of her way to say a prayer at her church. She asked for guidance because she considered the drone issue to be “a tipping point for our country.”

At the board meeting, she found only a handful of other residents, mostly there for other, more quotidian issues. They seemed surprised, Ms. Farmer thought, when Tareq Wafaie, an economic development manager for Amazon, delivered a presentation about Amazon’s Prime Air program. It would be the first drone delivery service in New England.

Mr. Wafaie explained that the drones are about five feet wide and five feet tall, have six arms with propellers, and can carry a single package that is five pounds or less. Customers opting in can get deliveries in 30 minutes or less, he said, with the drones dropping packages onto people’s yards or driveways from 13 feet up, without humans guiding them in real time.

The F.A.A., which governs the nation’s airspace, had cleared Amazon’s drone hub for up to 1,000 flights per day, from “about sunrise to sunset,” Mr. Wafaie said, and the drones can fly as far as 7.5 miles before circling back to their home base.

Ms. Farmer grabbed her phone and started calculating: If there were, say, 600 drone deliveries in 12 hours, that would mean almost one delivery every minute.

Several residents seemed to be thinking along similar lines. “The risk does not match the want,” Jen Parent, a teacher, told the board. “We’re at this point in our human history with technology, just because we can do it, doesn’t mean we should do it.”

One man said he couldn’t imagine the drones being quiet. Another said that drones were “cool,” but worried about privacy because their cameras could peer into yards.

A nervous Ms. Farmer fumbled with the microphone before taking it off its stand.

In a voice gentle enough to read bedtime stories, she explained that she had grown up in Winthrop, a town near Boston’s Logan Airport. Every day, all day long, she heard planes overhead.

“I just want to advise and really just say, you open the door to this and more will come,” she said to the planning board. “I implore that you continue to consider the sounds and the visuals. I love to walk. We love the nature.”

She added, “That’s why I moved here.”

The planning board postponed its decision. When Ms. Farmer got home, she told her husband, “Honey, this is not our wheelhouse. But we can’t stay silent.”

Steeped in the issue for what she called “a whole 30 seconds,” Ms. Farmer began posting about the drones on social media, to tell her neighbors.

At a Sept. 22 meeting of the select board, the town’s policymaking body, the public was allowed to speak about the issue and Ms. Farmer got up — twice — to oppose Amazon’s plan.

Once Amazon begins its service, “there’s no turning back,” she warned, citing communities in Louisiana, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas, where residents say they feel trapped after their cities approved Amazon’s plans.

The next day, Amazon held an informational session at a local hotel. Ms. Farmer sat in a corner to listen to other residents speak, amazed that a coalition against the drones had grown so quickly.

More than 200 people squeezed into the room, including residents from nearby towns that would be affected.

For nearly three hours, Mr. Wafaie, of Amazon, took questions from the crowd, saying that the drones were safe, popular and unobtrusive. He said the operation would start with about six of them (a decrease from the 10 to 12 he had discussed with the town in mid-August).

“We do hear a lot of feedback from our customers that we’re not fast enough, so that is the exact problem we’re trying to solve,” said Mr. Wafaie, who did not return an emailed request for comment. “Our customers are demanding this service.”

A lot of those, he added, are “single mothers who need diapers because they’re home with a sick child, and they can’t go out.”

The crowd groaned.

When Mr. Wafaie compared the drone noise to the sound made by someone holding an electric toothbrush, a high-pitched buzz filled the room. Someone had brought an electric toothbrush, and held it up. “That’s annoying!” said one woman.

“All day long, horrible!” another said.

For a second, Ms. Farmer laughed. Having watched many video posts of Amazon drones flying, she felt that the toothbrush came nowhere close to how loud they were.

Ms. Farmer has been sensitive to noise since sustaining a head injury in a car crash nearly a decade ago. When her neighbors mow their lawns or clear leaves with a blower, she has to run to the other side of her house. But at least those sounds fade quickly, she told herself. The drones would be relentless.

No one in the crowd spoke in favor of the drones. Instead, residents badgered Mr. Wafaie about safety, privacy and home values. Would Amazon would fly more drones and bigger ones? Could residents stop this program if they didn’t like it?

Several times, he said that they would not like his answer.

Amazon backing out of a drone hub wherever people don’t want it, he said, “would probably not happen.”

“We have a program that we are scaling,” he added.

Dan Kline, a Westborough resident, said in an interview that he assumed the company would have that stance. Scaling business, he said, is “what Amazon does.”

“There’s an air of arrogance that, ‘We’re Amazon and we’re going to this no matter what anyone says, or no matter what anyone wants,” he said. “But this is our town, not Amazon’s.”

The day after that informational session, Ms. Farmer and one of her old Westborough friends, Rod Jané, talked on the phone, in a panic.

It turned out that even before that first public meeting that Ms. Farmer attended in September, Amazon had already received a key ruling from the town.

Westborough’s building commissioner, William Hezlitt, had decided that Amazon’s proposed drone hub — which would replace parking spaces at their distribution center — was allowed by law, because it was an “accessory to the primary use,” as innocuous as, say, adding a carport to a home.

Mr. Hezlitt did not return a request for comment.

Mr. Jané, who works in economic and real estate development, and Ms. Farmer thought Mr. Hezlitt’s designation made no sense because the drone technology was wholly new. They thought Amazon should be required to obtain a special permit to use its property to fly drones. That would force the company to make a case for its drone hub, and the public would have a say.

They decided to contest the decision. By law, they had 30 days to appeal it. And they were on Day 29.

With the town hall closing at noon the next day, Mr. Jané and Ms. Farmer shifted into hyper speed. From their desks across town from each other, they began typing up and tweaking drafts of an appeal, sharing them by email.

By 5:30 a.m., they had an almost final version. They thought it would be smart to show that other residents supported it, so at 7 a.m., Ms. Farmer left home with a copy of the document and began flagging down people — in their cars, after morning Mass, on the street, jogging — to gather signatures. Twenty-five people signed.

Just after 10 a.m., she and Mr. Jané met outside of the town hall and walked together to the town clerk’s office, meeting their deadline with time to spare. “We did it,” he exclaimed, and both let out a long exhale.

The appeal hearing was scheduled for November, and Amazon’s project would be on hold until then. Other opposition was also gathering. With hundreds of residents now rebelling — many involved with Mass Blue Skies, a nonprofit started by Ms. Farmer and Mr. Jané and about 10 others — the town of Westborough made its own move to stop Amazon’s plans.

Some residents, including Mr. Jané, helped the town draft a bylaw that would restrict ground operations of any unmanned aircraft, “to protect the health, safety, privacy, peace, quiet enjoyment, property rights, and general welfare” of residents. It would bar drone launchpads, staging points and drop zones.

In October, more than 500 people packed the high school auditorium to vote on the bylaw.

There was a retired mechanic in his 70s. A homemaker in her 30s. Tech workers and cashiers. Longtime residents living in houses from the 1800s, and new neighbors in apartment buildings.

In interviews at the meeting, nearly two dozen people said that the vote meant more than just trying to stop Amazon.

The residents said their votes stood for quiet weekend mornings hiking the Charm Bracelet trails that encircle the town. And peaceful afternoons sipping tea on their neighbor’s picnic table. And lolling in the privacy of their backyard, maybe even sunbathing nude.

The bylaw passed, 510-13.

As residents left the high school, Ms. Farmer had tears in her eyes as she grabbed people — some complete strangers — to hug them.

The Massachusetts attorney general said it has until Jan. 20 to decide whether to approve the new bylaw. But the vote already has had an effect.

At the end of October, just days before a hearing on Ms. Farmer’s and Mr. Jané’s appeal of the decision on accessory use, Amazon asked the town to withdraw its application for the drone hub, but asserted the right to come back with a new plan. The building commissioner then withdrew his own decision.

For now, it remains Westborough, 1, Amazon, 0.
