item.title: Democrats Nominate Jeffries as Speaker, Making History
item.description:
House Democrats on Wednesday nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be speaker, voting overwhelmingly over resistance from the left to put him in line to become the first Black lawmaker to hold the post.

The election by secret ballot came just over two weeks after Mr. Jeffries, 56, who has led House Democrats since 2022, presided over sweeping victories for his party, which won a historically large majority in the midterm elections.

The vote was 251 to 11, with two Democrats abstaining, according to a person who attended the confidential session and detailed the results on the condition of anonymity. The margin demonstrated the breadth of Mr. Jeffries’s backing in a large and ideologically diverse caucus.

Accepting the nomination, he paid homage to the civil rights hero and long-serving Representative John Lewis of Georgia, who frequently exhorted people to get in “good trouble” fighting injustice.

“It’s a ‘good trouble’ moment in America,” Mr. Jeffries told the assembled Democrats.

He will still have to be elected on the House floor in January, when he will need a majority of members in the chamber to rise and say his name to formally win the post that is second in line to the presidency. But the lopsided secret-ballot vote suggested he will have more than enough support to do so.

Mr. Jeffries’s nomination was almost a foregone conclusion; no Democrat emerged to challenge him, and even some of his loudest critics ultimately did not want to publicly oppose the man in line to be the nation’s first Black speaker.

His frictionless ascent counted as a rarity in the House, where party leaders often rise through tumultuous challenges.

“It’s a good day,” said Representative Steny Hoyer of Maryland, the former No. 2 Democrat, as he headed into the closed-door session. “I served with the first woman speaker of the House. Now we’re going to elect the first African American speaker of the House.” Mr. Hoyer said it was a testimony to the country’s progress.

Inside the room, according to a person who was present, Representative James E. Clyburn, Democrat of South Carolina, gave the final speech nominating Mr. Jeffries, invoking Mr. Lewis, who died in 2020, as he reflected on the significance of elevating a Black man for the job.

Still, Mr. Jeffries faced loud grass-roots resistance from progressives fed up with the Democratic Party establishment who see Mr. Jeffries, a reserved moderate and prodigious fund-raiser, as an avatar of the status quo who is beholden to corporate interests.

Progressives who want Democrats to cut off U.S. aid to Israel and who champion “Medicare for all” said they were concerned that Mr. Jeffries, a longtime supporter of the Jewish state who they view as too closely aligned with AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group, would stand in the way of their demands.

In a statement, a group of newly elected democratic socialist lawmakers said they voted against Mr. Jeffries because their constituents sent them to Congress with a “mandate” to deliver change on “Medicare for all, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics” and “ending the genocide in Gaza.” While the group acknowledged some “meaningful progress” in their conversations with Mr. Jeffries, they said they still opposed him.

The group included Representatives-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York; Adam Hamawy of New Jersey; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

Mr. Jeffries, who in recent days met with almost all members and newly elected Democrats as he sought to wrap up his nomination with as little opposition as possible, is known for his cautious and highly disciplined style.

He likes to host listening sessions and have a caucus “family discussion” before telegraphing his stance on any issue. But he also appears willing to move in response to broad calls for bold action.

On Tuesday, for instance, less than 24 hours before his nomination, Mr. Jeffries endorsed a broad expansion of Medicare to cover more Americans and a wider variety of services, edging closer to the Medicare for all proposal championed by progressives.

It was a sign that with a larger majority giving him more room to maneuver and progressives pressing him to take up a bolder agenda, he saw the need and opportunity to take a more ambitious approach.

Mr. Jeffries, who grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, first ran for the State Legislature at 29. He was always viewed by people around him as a potential national leader, though he had been hesitant to reflect on the significance of his place in history until he had the vote wrapped up.

“Over the last four years, that pressure has already been on me,” he said in an interview earlier this month, when asked if he felt the weight of breaking a racial barrier. “Failure is not an option.”

Despite the sweeping electoral victories, Mr. Jeffries has been facing loud resistance to his leadership. Many lawmakers said their phone lines had been blowing up with constituents demanding a new face to lead the party as it takes control of Congress. But even amid that pressure, many of the progressives in Congress said they thought Mr. Jeffries deserved a chance to lead them in the majority.

item.title: The Anti-A.I. Campus Movement Is Growing
item.description:
Last March, a handful of students at Transylvania University created a petition, attempting to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus. It asked the administration to cancel chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and instead invest the money in “human-centered education.”

About a third of the college’s students signed on.

Transylvania, in Lexington, Ky., is tiny, with under 1,000 students. But across the country and the globe, there has been a swell of campus resistance to A.I., including a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A.I. at all.

Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work. College leaders have generally embraced A.I., saying it is key to preparing students for the work force.

But as A.I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down.

Much of the opposition comes from the political left, and focuses on how A.I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices in opposition are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations.

But there are also deep concerns that A.I. degrades the experience of college itself, by removing the productive struggle of learning.

Resistors from California to Sydney to Paris are increasingly publishing manifestoes that lay out demands: that colleges not partner with A.I. companies; that professors not be required to use generative A.I. in lessons or grading; and that students be allowed to refuse to complete assignments that require the use of chatbots, without any impact on their grades.

At the University of Kentucky, a research employee who described himself as a humanist successfully applied for a religious exemption from using A.I.

Alice Beatty, 22, helped lead the Transylvania petition drive as a senior last spring. The student newspaper had called attention to the $120,000 the university paid to purchase licenses to ChatGPT and Gemini, chatbots from OpenAI and Google. And Ms. Beatty had participated in a discussion group formed by several A.I.-skeptical professors.

She noted that even before Transylvania provided free access to chatbots, A.I. had been everywhere on campus. Students used it to summarize readings, break down physics problems and compose discussion-board posts and papers that they were supposed to be writing the old-fashioned way, on their own.

Yet when Ms. Beatty and some classmates stood near the dining hall to collect signatures on the petition, almost everyone they spoke to signed.

“I use A.I.,” she recalled some peers telling her, “and I am ashamed I use it.”

A spokeswoman for Transylvania University declined an interview request but said that professors were free to either embrace A.I., limit its use or ban it entirely in their classes.

For students, ethical and practical questions about A.I. will be part of the world they enter after graduating, she said by email.

Vague and confusing college A.I. policies have helped create the conscientious objector movement, said Hollis Robbins, an English professor at the University of Utah who writes often about A.I. and education. She suggested that colleges stop grading take-home assignments that are easy to cheat on with A.I., and shut down online courses that have become rife with academic misconduct in the A.I. era.

If institutions took those steps, she argued, students might be more curious and hopeful about the technology.

“There is silence about these major tech issues,” she said. “Students just seeing grown-ups being inconsistent and letting them down.”

Georgetown University began offering students and faculty free access to Gemini in March. At the time, like many institutions, Georgetown generally allowed each professor to set their own A.I. rules.

Yet in focus groups on A.I. conducted by the university, students asked for clearer guidance. They were worried about cognitive offloading, cheating and A.I. providing false information. Forty percent of the student sentiment was cautious or negative toward A.I., according to the university, compared with 25 percent that was positive or hopeful.

Georgetown’s student newspaper published an editorial criticizing the Gemini license, arguing that it tacitly pushed students toward technology that is often used to plagiarize and avoid academic effort.

This fall, the university is changing its approach. Under a new president, Eduardo M. Peñalver, it announced it would form a faculty committee to come up with clearer principles on A.I. use. For Georgetown, a Jesuit institution, Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical on the risks of A.I. will be an important influence.

Dr. Peñalver said in an interview that Georgetown would seek to make course expectations around A.I. more transparent and provide more tech-free spaces on campus. Oral presentations, discussion groups and in-person tests would become more important, he said, to protect “from the intrusion of this technology.”

Still, the university will continue to expand free access to A.I. tools, which he said had the potential to do good.

“We’re not interested in pushing people to use A.I. in ways that don’t align with their values,” Dr. Peñalver said. “But I certainly encourage people to learn about it.”

“Even if you’re opposed to this technology,” he added, “that awareness and understanding is important to the success of your project.”

Many conscientious objectors, though, say they try to avoid generative A.I. as much as possible, blocking it from their devices and not experimenting with it in their own work.

Emily Tucker, executive director of the Center on Privacy and Technology at Georgetown Law School, has been a leader in organizing resistance to A.I. use on campus. She has also signed an open letter with 1,300 other educators “who refuse the call for generative A.I. adoption in schools and colleges, and reject the narrative of its inevitability.”

Law students have told her they feared that if they didn’t use A.I. to speed their output, they would be outpaced in class and at work by those who did. But Professor Tucker said that using A.I. degrades a student’s ability to read and analyze dense legal texts, and risks incorrect citations of case law.

“It’s not useful,” said Professor Tucker, who said she rarely uses A.I. herself, though she acknowledged it might help in some tasks, like seeking specific information within a large set of documents.

At Cornell, Shimon Edelman, a psychology professor who holds a Ph.D. in computer science, has also signed the anti-A.I. letter. He lets students decide whether or not to use A.I., though he warns them it could degrade deeper learning.

He said he had been dismayed to see the Cornell administration greet A.I. warmly, as an “essential tool,” instead of warning more forcefully against its risks. In October, Cornell announced free access to chatbots, A.I. coding tools and agentic A.I.

“It’s unthinkable,” Professor Edelman said of using A.I. in his own research, even when he faced having to read 800 documents for a recent book project.

Emmali Simmelink, a senior studying classics and religion at Whitman College in Washington State, said students on her campus sometimes plug classroom discussion prompts directly into ChatGPT.

“If you can’t generate a coherent thought without ChatGPT, I genuinely lose a lot of respect for you,” she said. She added, laughing, “I am really insufferable about this.”

She said she brings up concerns about the environmental impact of A.I. as soon as she hears somebody say, “I asked ChatGPT.”

The topic can be divisive socially, so much so, several students said, that friend groups often develop a shared view of A.I.

Preston Hicks, 26, is studying history and education at Rider University in New Jersey — a second degree, after he worked previously as a software developer. He said many of his friends are artists who instinctually oppose A.I., a view he often shares.

But he can also imagine using A.I. in his future career as a teacher, to handle paperwork and other logistical tasks.

“I am more nuanced,” he said. “If I see a good use, I will use it.”

item.title: Trump Grows Frustrated With Vance Over Iran War Critique
item.description:
At first, President Trump appeared notably unfazed by Vice President JD Vance’s post-election analysis blaming the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.

“I think it’s largely true,” the president told reporters after Mr. Vance posted a lengthy missive on social media in which he also critiqued much of the administration’s messaging in the run-up to the elections.

But over the past two weeks, Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how his vice president framed his assessment of what went wrong, complaining to aides and allies that Mr. Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran, according to people with knowledge of the president’s comments.

At the same time, Mr. Trump has continued to praise Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, in private conversations and suggesting that he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe discussions going on behind closed doors. Mr. Trump’s allies have noted that Mr. Rubio has repeatedly said the president’s move to attack Iran was essential for the country’s national security.

Mr. Trump has hinted at his irritation with Mr. Vance in public, saying earlier this month that the vice president should have “made one other statement.”

“If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” he said, laying out what he believes was missing from Mr. Vance’s analysis.

The tension comes at a critical juncture for Mr. Vance, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028, a campaign in which Mr. Trump’s support could be critical to his ability to secure the Republican nomination. The president’s favorable comments about Mr. Rubio are the latest example of how Mr. Trump has been weighing the strengths of the two men as the question of his successor grows more urgent.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Mr. Vance’s office declined to comment, pointing to recent interviews the vice president has given.

When asked on Fox News this week about his post-election commentary and whether there was any “daylight” between him and the president, Mr. Vance said, “I think there’s no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration.”

On Wednesday, Mr. Vance canceled a planned appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit, citing meetings in Washington to address the recent tech outages.

Since Mr. Trump brought him aboard as his running mate for a second term, many Republicans have assumed that Mr. Vance, a former senator from Ohio, would be the front-runner for their party’s nomination in 2028. But Mr. Trump has waffled publicly and privately on his vice president throughout his tenure, and Mr. Vance says he has not decided whether to run for president.

“I haven’t made a decision,” he said on Fox News. “We’ll figure it out sometime next year.”

Allies of Mr. Vance, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, say he is genuinely undecided about his political future. They point to his young family (his fourth child was born in July) as one reason he might not mount a White House bid in 2028. They also note his obsession with political analysis and data and suggest that if he does not see a path to victory, he may sit out this race.

The fallout from the war with Iran — and its unpopularity among voters — could be a significant factor, too. Some allies of Mr. Vance say that if the president decides to resume major combat operations in Iran, it would drastically reduce Mr. Vance’s chances of running.

The vice president, who endorsed Mr. Trump in 2023 saying he would not drag the United States into new wars, expressed reservations about the conflict privately inside the administration. But after the huge G.O.P. losses in this month’s midterms, he went public, laying out in blunt terms what he said went wrong.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in his lengthy social media post the day after the midterms.

Mr. Vance made the point of adding that Mr. Trump had also said as much — though the president has blamed Republicans’ losses on many factors, chiefly that he was not on the ticket.

For Mr. Vance, it appeared to be an attempt to separate himself from the administration’s policy without criticizing the president. But Mr. Trump soon announced that he was pulling his vice president from engaging in peace talks with Iran, an effort that Mr. Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Mr. Trump said he wanted Mr. Vance to focus on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, who worked in Mr. Trump’s White House during the first term and is now a co-host of “The View,” said that comment from Mr. Vance reminded her of a comment that Kamala Harris, then the vice president, made on the ABC show during the 2024 campaign. When asked if she would have done anything differently from President Joseph R. Biden Jr., Ms. Harris said, “There is not a thing that comes to mind.”

“JD Vance is in the impossible position that any Trump V.P. inevitably ends up in,” Ms. Griffin said. “He can’t have any separation or daylight from the president.”

Mr. Vance’s “daylight” comment this week “may have seemed insignificant in the moment, but it will live in campaign ads,” she added.

Mr. Vance’s allies say a competitive primary, not a coronation, will determine the next Republican presidential nominee, and they cite Ms. Harris’s loss in 2024 as evidence of that theory. Ms. Harris quickly secured the Democratic nomination after Mr. Biden dropped out of the race, despite some Democrats’ calls for a more formal nominating process.

But Mr. Vance ultimately could find himself in a similar situation to Ms. Harris, who many voters saw as an extension of Mr. Biden, political strategists said. Even as she privately signaled she had concerns about Mr. Biden’s handling of the Israel-Hamas war, she was unable to figure out how to separate herself from the unpopular president.

“It’s very hard to get me to say that I have any amount of sympathy for JD Vance because he put himself in this position,” said Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and former deputy campaign manager to Ms. Harris. “But you do have to feel for him because he’s stuck. When you’re the vice president, you’re stuck. In the Harris situation, there was not much you can actually do to separate yourself.”

Mr. Vance now must wrestle with that complex dynamic as he assesses the future of the Republican Party and in which direction he would try to lead it. His path to the vice presidency — from a “never Trumper” to Mr. Trump’s vice president — suggests that he could go in different directions.

Mr. Vance was an avowed critic of Mr. Trump in 2016, calling him “unfit for our nation’s highest office.” He then became a supporter of Mr. Trump and sought the president’s endorsement when he ran for a Senate seat in Ohio in 2022. He received the endorsement and won that race.

Many Republicans believe Mr. Vance would need the explicit, or at least implicit, support from Mr. Trump to win a Republican primary. But that is far from a guarantee. The president has always relished competition among his aides, and his advisers say he is in no rush to endorse a successor.

And after Republicans’ disastrous results in the elections this month, in which Democrats won the largest midterm victory for either party since the post-Watergate elections, other Republicans see an opening, too. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida are among those considering possible bids.

Then there’s Mr. Rubio. He has said he would support Mr. Vance and dismissed reports that he is going to leave the administration to run for president. But some of his allies said he would run if Mr. Trump encouraged him to do so — and Mr. Trump has not been shy about lavishing praise on him.

“How hot is Marco, right?” Mr. Trump said Tuesday at the ASEAN summit in Manila. “Is Marco doing a great job? He’s been fantastic.”

While Mr. Vance has remained in the United States, as the vice president does when the president travels abroad, Mr. Rubio is playing a prominent role on the president’s trip. On Tuesday, he addressed public fears about the multiple technology outages in the United States, seeking to reassure Americans that there was no evidence of cyberattacks.

Mr. Rubio’s defense of the Iran war, in particular, has earned him good will with the president.

In a recent interview with The Times, Mr. Rubio said Mr. Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for authorizing strikes against Iran.

“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.

The distinct approaches of Mr. Rubio and Mr. Vance underscore a broader debate in the party — should the next Republican presidential candidate align themselves with Mr. Trump’s legacy?

Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey, who himself is considering another run for the White House, said Mr. Vance’s challenges transcend his unique position as vice president.

“I don’t think anyone that was part of Trump 2.0 will be able to win in the fall of 2028,” he said. “They will be billed as another four years of Donald Trump, and that will not be salable to the American people.”
